#2745. Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins preview, prediction: On Paper

The Detroit Lions are beat up after a physical and emotional win over the Minnesota Vikings. And while they must travel to play a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team, they can't afford to underestimate them. The NFC North is too competitive for a trap game, and the Dolphins are a little scrappier than they appear.

But is there a real chance of an upset in Miami, or are the Lions clearly the better team? Let's examine it in our Lions vs. Dolphins preview and prediction. It's time for On Paper.

The Lions' passing offense remains one of their most reliable units on the team. While last week's performance against the Vikings wasn't explosive, it was certainly a lot better than most teams manage against Minnesota's defense. While the DVOA ranking remains outside the top five, I still believe Detroit's passing attack should be in that top tier.

Detroit is humming in all facets of their passing attack. In pass protection, the Lions allow the fifth-lowest pressure percentage (30.1%), rank seventh in pass-block win rate (54%), and rank third in PFF team pass-blocking grade (75.1).

The Dolphins may have a worse pass defense than the Lions. Five out of the seven quarterbacks who have faced Miami have finished with a passer rating of 119.8 or higher. Granted, they've played some really good quarterbacks in Brock Purdy, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Drake Maye. Still, those quarterbacks have outperformed their year-long efficiency against Miami, and the DVOA ranking—which adjusts to opponents' strength—proves this is a bad pass defense.

This is the result of having an extremely young and inexperienced back seven.

Though there is some recent hope for Miami's pass rush. As Erik Schlitt pointed out in his Honolulu Blueprint, while the season-long stats don't look great for the Dolphins' ability to get to the passer (35.6% pressure rate, 18th; 4.2% sack rate, 28th), they've started to put things together. All nine of their sacks have come in the last four games, and they've posted a pressure rate of 39.5% or higher in three out of four of those games (league average is around 36%).

Over those last four games, the Dolphins' pass defense has been better, but certainly not good. From Weeks 4-8, Miami ranks 27th in dropback EPA (0.180) and 29th in success rate (50.7%).

Player to watch: Sam LaPorta. It's been a quiet few weeks for the Lions tight end, but Miami is allowing the sixth-highest yardage to tight ends (483 yards) and tied for the fourth-most touchdowns (six).

Advantage: Lions +3. This is a top-five unit vs. a bottom-five unit. The only reason I'm not giving it a higher advantage is that some things are trending Miami's way, and weather could also play a factor, with some slight chance of rain.

The Lions' rushing attack still has frustrating bouts of inconsistency, but last week's performance against the Vikings felt like a revelation. Whether Detroit's sidecar formation was a Vikings-specific answer or the cracking of the code for the entire season, we'll see. But it shows one thing for certain: Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is capable of finding some answers.

For the season, the Lions rushing attack now ranks:

But I must continue to repeat myself that the negative plays are a big problem. The Lions' 19.3% stuffed rate is sixth in the NFL. Those figures are down from last week (20.9%, third-highest), but it still remains an issue to track. Detroit's power success rank also improved after last week, but they still rank just 24th, converting on just 59% of short-yardage situations.

Still, it's worth pointing out how both the offensive line and the running backs are doing their parts. Detroit's line ranks third in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and fourth in PFF run blocking grade. Meanwhile, Detroit's backfield ranks sixth in rushing yards over expected per rush (+0.5), sixth in yards after contact per rush (3.38), and Jahmyr Gibbs ranks fourth in missed tackle forced rate (31.9%).

This chart doesn't exactly vibe with the Dolphins' bottom-10 DVOA ranking. They're not giving up a ton of yards nor a ton of yards per carry. So what gives? Let's look deeper.

In short, it appears the Dolphins don't give up a ton of big, explosive plays, but they essentially give up exactly what the offense needs. That's backed by data. Miami has only given up 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th), and just three rushes of 20+ yards (t-sixth fewest).

The good news is the Dolphins are weak where the Lions' run offense struggles. They've produced just a 14.9% stuffed rate (23rd), and they rank 21st in power success rate, allowing conversions on 68% of short-yardage situations.

Player to watch: Jacob Rodriguez. The Dolphins rookie linebacker has been a fun player to watch thus far. Rodriguez has been credited with 30 "stops" per PFF (plays that are a failure for offense), which is second most among ALL NFL linebackers, not just rookies. Seventeen of those have come in the run, t-eighth most.

Advantage: Lions +1.5. I'm not sure I'd expect a huge game from Gibbs and company, given that Miami has not allowed over 150 rushing yards in a game. But Detroit should be fairly efficient on the ground.

It hasn't been a great start to the year for Malik Willis in his new home, but it's hard to blame him given the supporting cast. He's got an extremely young receiving corps, a new offensive system, and an imbalanced offensive line. As a result, the Dolphins rank:

The Dolphins aren't a complete disaster, but they're clearly below average.

That said, there are some very interesting advanced statistics surrounding Willis. For one, he's not afraid to chuck it deep. He currently owns the third-highest average depth of target (9.2), and his deep ball percentage of 16.4% ranks first in the NFL (yes, above Jordan Love, too). But he also ranks third in time to throw (3.05), suggesting he likely holds onto the ball too long—especially when you consider the Dolphins have the second-highest sack rate (10.3%).

The offensive line is a mixed bag. Though they've allowed the second-highest pressure rate (43.2%), they rank 20th in pass block win rate and 31st in PFF pass blocking grade. The issue is that the left side of their offensive line is good-to-great (LT Patrick Paul is 14th in pass blocking grade, rookie LG Kadyn Proctor is improving) and the right side is a disaster (RT Austin Jackson is dead last in pass blocking grade, RG Jonah Savaiinaea is 63rd out of 76).

And as mentioned before, the receiving corps is ridiculously young: Malik Washington is 25; Caleb Douglas is 23, and Chris Bell is 22. Young doesn't mean bad, but it'll take them some time to get adjusted to the NFL.

Is the Lions' pass defense actually getting better? It's hard for me to tell. The raw numbers are improving, but as the chart above shows, they've also played some pretty bad passing offenses in the last few weeks. I'm not yet convinced.

I think it's also worth noting that the Lions' pass rush has fallen off a bit as of late. After three weeks, the Lions ranked 10th in pressure rate (39.0%) and second in time to pressure (2.46). The Lions now rank just 17th in pressure rate (35.8%) and 20th in time to pressure (2.68). And this week, they're almost certainly without DJ Wonnum, who was fourth on the team in pressures (14). That said, the Lions still do rank third in pass rush win rate, third in PFF pass rush grade, and seventh in sack rate. I just worry it's trending in the wrong direction.

Then, of course, there are the injuries to account for. While it looks like Brian Branch is on track to play, the Lions don't have MIKE linebacker Jack Campbell, and top cornerback D.J. Reed is trending toward missing this game. Detroit's back seven has already struggled immensely in coverage, and now they'll be tested further.

Player to watch: Malik Washington. Washington leads the Dolphins in catches (31) and yards (329), and the Dolphins like to use him all over the field—as a screen weapon or downfield. His 4.47 speed is a weapon.

Advantage: Draw. I'm not particularly impressed with either unit. I think it's certainly possible Willis hits on a few big downfield plays, and I think it's also very possible Detroit is able to disrupt and sack Willis 4-6 times this game. In the end, I think it'll all even out.

This is another weird statistical oddity for Miami. By the charts, it looks like they actually have a good thing going with their run game, including a breakout season from Ollie Gordon (408 yards, 4.5 YPC, 4 TDs) and some quarterback rushing potential from Malik Willis (225 yards, 3 TDs). Yet, the advanced statistics aren't as impressive. They rank:

It turns out this rushing attack is very boom or bust—like a less-efficient version of Detroit's running game. They have produced t-sixth-most rushes of 10+ yards (26), but also a 19.1% stuff rate—seventh-highest.

The problem appears to be that the offensive line isn't carrying their end of the bargain. They rank 26th in run block win rate, 27th in PFF run blocking grade, and 27th in adjusted line yards.

But credit to Gordon for doing everything he can to get the most out of his situation.

I don't know, man. The Lions are just too inconsistent in the run game this year. They've been better lately, but it seems like they're still susceptible to explosive plays. Overall, the Lions rank:

So that pretty much matches my eye test. They're decent down-to-down, but they give up too many explosives. Though they've only allowed 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th fewest), they've allowed six of 20+ yards (t-ninth most).

And with the loss of Jack Campbell, it's hard to know how this unit will respond. Detroit has an experienced linebacking corps in Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske, but none provide the instincts and consistency of Campbell.

Advantage: Dolphins +1. I'm giving Miami a slight advantage here for a couple of reasons. Second, I do think Willis provides a legitimate rushing threat, and Detroit has lost contain far too often this year. Third, I just think Miami is better than their stats suggest, and the Lions may be a tad worse. It shouldn't be a dominant day for Miami—and if Detroit can get out to a big lead, they can erase this advantage completely—but I still think Miami has the slight edge here.

On Paper drops to 5-2 overall and 3-4 against the spread, but I don't feel all that bad for how my Lions vs. Vikings preview played out. The only area I made a clear mistake was underestimating the Lions' run game, and for the first half of that game, I looked right. But Petzing made a lot of believers on Sunday, and I'm one of them.

#2742. Luka Garza is making life easier for the Celtics

Hours before the Boston Celtics and Milwaukee Bucks faced off Wednesday night, Luka Garza was already getting to work. He joined the team's Stay Ready crew, warming up alongside Mitchell Robinson and Jordan Walsh while his father, Frank, watched from courtside near the baseline.

Garza wasn't in Boston's Jayson Tatum-less starting lineup, but that didn't matter. His routine remained the same.

That's standard for Garza. Each night, he knows the moment could arrive when Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla calls his number. On Wednesday, it came early, with 5:37 remaining in the first quarter. He checked in for Hugo González and knocked down his first shot — a wide-open 3-pointer from the wing — to extend Boston's lead over Milwaukee to 25-8.

Down the other end, less than a minute later, Garza came away with a steal. Payton Pritchard capitalized on the extra possession by draining a jumper. Garza knocked down each of his three 3-point attempts to lead the Celtics with 11 points at halftime. Mazzulla didn't turn to him nearly as much in the second half, but he had already made his impact felt.

In just 18 minutes against Milwaukee, Garza reinforced his reliability.

Oct 14, 2026; Boston, Massachusetts, USA; Boston Celtics center Luka Garza (52) shoots the ball during warmups prior to a game against the Charlotte Hornets at TD Garden. Mandatory Credit: Bob DeChiara-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

He went from playing 8.9 minutes per game through the first five games of the season to averaging 18.7 over the last three against Orlando, Houston and Milwaukee. In return, Garza has rewarded Mazzulla's increased deployment of the 27-year-old veteran, posting averages of 12.3 points, 4.7 rebounds, and two assists since the start of November.

Throughout it all, Garza has maintained his knack for creating second chances on the offensive glass. He's grabbed 15 offensive rebounds, just behind Robinson (17) and Neemias Queta (18) for the team lead. He's also re-emerged as a dangerous 3-point threat, much like last season. His 52.4% clip from beyond the arc leads the Celtics and ranks first among Eastern Conference centers averaging at least 2.6 attempts.

From the corners, Garza has shot 6-of-8, going 11-of-21 overall from three through the first eight games this season.

The drive-and-kick option for teammates like Paul George and Pritchard to find Garza on the perimeter was utilized Wednesday night, and it's proven to be an effective one. Garza is Mazzulla's best 3-point shooter among Boston's centers, making him a legitimate outside shooting threat that opposing defenses can't afford to leave unattended.

Entering a season where Queta vs. Robinson starting center debates dominated the discourse surrounding Boston's front court, Garza has quietly made his case to play each night. He's done his part to support the group amid Robinson's early-season adjustment struggles by remaining prepared to contribute. And despite understanding what playing behind Queta and Robinson could mean for his minutes on any given night, Garza has emerged as a leader by example in Boston's reserve unit.

The Celtics can call on him to perform alongside the starters while also counting on him to work with those coming off the bench. Garza occupies something of an older brother role in helping teammates navigate the same challenges he previously faced during his three-year stint with the Minnesota Timberwolves.

In Boston, he's able to simultaneously shine and stay hungry.

It doesn't take much for Garza to make a difference either. Sometimes it'll go unnoticed when he battles for a second-chance opportunity because the Celtics fail to convert. Other times, he might not get the seven 3-point attempts he did in Houston. But the effort is always there.

This season, he's averaging 7.5 points with 3.1 rebounds on 48.7 percent shooting. That doesn't even begin to tell half the story of what he's been doing on the floor.

The Celtics can't offer Garza 60-plus starts, but the coaching staff remains vigilant at all times. His impact off the bench has been rewarded, sending the message that the team is well aware of what he's brought to the table. That's certainly encouraging for Garza, who's begun to carve out a role in a Boston front court that was heavily considered crowded throughout much of the offseason.

#2741. England amateur cricketer banned 2 years in cheating scandal

An amateur cricketer in England has been banned for two years in a cheating scandal caught on video.

The allegations came to light in July when a video showed a fielder clicking his fingers to imitate the sound of a bat connecting with the ball before a player is called out.

The North Yorkshire & South Durham Cricket League launched an investigation into the player and the second-division Saltburn team. It spent weeks interviewing players and reviewing video footage.

"Charges were subsequently brought against the player and Saltburn C.C.," the league said in a statement Friday. "Both admitted the charges."

The player, identified across British media as Brian Devine, was suspended from all cricket under the jurisdiction of the England and Wales Cricket Board for a two-year period through late September 2028.

"This covers playing, coaching, umpiring, scoring and managing junior teams," the league said.

The Saltburn team was relegated to division three and will start next season with 60-point deduction. The club also has been fined 300 pounds ($400).

"The league recognizes the strain this has placed on many people, especially those who were abused online and in person. We ask everyone to respect that the formal process is now complete," the league said.

Cricket has had its share of scandals, ranging from the so-called "Sandpapergate" ball-tampering episode in 2018 that led to suspensions for three Australian international players, to spot fixing scandals that have led to lengthy bans.

But at the amateur levels, such as this so-called village cricket competition in England, umpires have no access to video replays to make decisions and there's a level of trust required from players when claiming catches.

A cricket umpire could be fooled into calling a player out if they believed they heard the sound of the ball clipping the edge of a bat before being caught.

British media dubbed the case "Clicky Ponting," a play on the name of Australian great Ricky Ponting.

#2740. An All-22 look inside the blitzing arsenal of Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores

A game against the Vikings means your offense will get the full Brian Flores Experience, a blitz-crazed defense that sends two or three extra rushers at your offensive line…all game.

That's what the Buffalo Bills have in front of them on Monday Night Football in Week 9. Entering this contest, Minnesota owns the league's highest blitz rate (on dropbacks) at 74.2%. The Commanders are second at 44.5%, and the league average is 31.2%. Minnesota blitzes frequently on run plays too.

Let's dig into the ingenuity of Flores' enormous blitzing arsenal.

We'll begin in Week 1, Minnesota's game against Jordan Love and the Packers.

What you'll see below is Vikings in an overload look to the left side of the Packers offensive front… with four defenders on the line of scrimmage on that side of the ball, compared to just two on the other side of the center.

But at the snap is when the calculated chaos ensued.

Cornerback Byron Murphy, who initially looked to be covering Christian Watson in a tight split near the numbers on the upper portion of the screen, screamed off the edge as a blitzer.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the defensive front, Andrew Van Ginkel, floated backward into coverage, and cornerback Isaiah Rodgers is actually the furthest outside blitzer.

With the all the down linemen sliding left, it provided Rodgers a free run into the backfield:

Watch again, and notice how the Packers tight end Josh Whyle — originally in motion —was ready for Rodgers and picked him up as he cut back toward the left side of Green Bay's line.

However, because his blocking assignment drew him in that direction, he wasn't positioned to help the right side of the Packers front that suddenly featured a right tackle stretched exceptionally wide by Murphy's cornerback blitz and Minnesota's most purely gifted outside rusher Dallas Turner erupting past the right guard.

Even when an offensive line thinks it picks up the blitzer Flores intended to get a free run, there's often a secondary hole opened for another defender to disrupt the pocket.

Flores absolutely will show all-out, eight-man pressure in this game. It's one of his trademarks. That doesn't always mean eight defenders are entering the rush on that play. In fact, that rarely happens. Discerning which defender(s) will drop into coverage is the challenge, particularly as the game clock is winding down.

Like here, against the Packers, the Vikings showed an eight-pass pressure package. Behind that hyper-aggressive look was plenty of green grass before three defensive backs roughly 10 yards beyond the line of scrimmage, splitting the field into thirds.

Pay close attention to what transpired at the snap and a split second later. The two outer most rushers on the left side of their defensive front show blitz but never actually rushed the quarterback, and linebacker Blake Cashman dropped into coverage underneath. On the edge, Van Ginkel watched the quarterback and kept contain.

Jordan Love missed a wide-open out-breaking route at the 40 yard line because he's forced into a quick decision which ultimately was a deep-ball attempt toward Christian Watson that was nearly intercepted.

The takeaway from that blitz is critical. Quite naturally, the Vikings have to drop at least one defender toward the side of the field with more receivers.

That feature of Minnesota's blitzes is noteworthy. It's the one distinct way an offense's pass game can dictate to the Vikings defense.

Note here, on this blitz against the Buccaneers, how linebacker Eric Wilson sunk at the snap toward the side of the field with three receivers for Tampa Bay.

And, sometimes, the sinking defender (occasionally it's two defenders) take three or four steps to sell blitz before retreating into a short zone.

There are two receivers to Jared Goff's right in this pre-snap alignment. At the snap, and even a second after it, the Vikings made a convincing case for an an all-out, eight-man pressure. But the blitz only featured seven, as Cashman exploded forward, disappeared into the middle of Detroit's offensive line then dropped into the middle of the field to take away Jahmyr Gibbs' underneath route.

In those all-out blitz looks, even if the Vikings ultimately send six or seven rushers — which is still an extremely high amount of rushers toward the quarterback — it's beneficial for the offense to feature as many routes with quick breaks off the vertical stem as possible.

On that specific play, notice how Jameson Williams and Amon Ra-St. Brown ran vertically and didn't have their heads fully turned around as Goff was being sacked.

Sure, the Lions were in a seven-man protection, but the offense can't assume every blocker will find his exact assignment in a flash after the snap.

And I've saved the most creative Flores blitz for last.

This came on a sack of Daniel Jones against the Colts.

Rather unusually, the Vikings were clearly in man coverage across the board — they've used man just 7.2% of the time, the lowest rate in the league and well below the NFL average of 22.4%. And it wasn't an all-out pressure look, as it was reasonably easy to discern Minnesota's five "known rushers" before the snap.

But pay close attention to the defender second-furthest from the left edge along Minnesota's front. It's Cashman, and at the snap, he started toward the Colts right tackle, as if he was going to deploy a stunt with edge rusher Dallas Turner. After selling the DT-DE stunt — Cash was effectively a defensive tackle on that play — he planted his foot in the ground to change directions completely and loop all the way through the A gap.

Unsurprisingly Cashman got a free run at Jones and registered the sack.

I don't believe I've ever seen that type of blitz before. That's not to say it's the first of its kind in NFL history, yet that type of creativity with one defender is exceptionally rare.

Imagine an entire offensive line group, extra blocking help in the backfield, and the quarterback processing everything in front of them in roughly 10-15 seconds after breaking the huddle and then again in one second after the snap.

It's precisely what makes facing this Flores defense so difficult.

Offenses know they're going to blitz on almost every snap.

But the Vikings don't care if they're predictable because they have such a wide variety of blitzes to stress the offensive communication throughout the duration of each contest.

#2737. Carlos Prates: Makhachev and Khabib booking fights when they want is not the right way

Carlos Prates accuses Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov of being inactive champions.

Prates (24-7 MMA, 7-1 UFC) was furious when welterweight champion Makhachev opted not to fight him at UFC 336. As a result, Prates will face Michael Morales (19-0 MMA, 7-0 UFC) for the interim belt on Jan. 30 in Toronto.

While Nurmagomedov defended his lightweight title once a year, Makhachev (29-1 MMA, 18-1 UFC) has been more active. He had two title fights in 2023 and 2025.

"I think Khabib and Islam, they're the same," Prates said in an interview with Squawka. "They book fights when they want, when they feel really good. Of course, it's OK – they are the champs. When Khabib was champ, he did the same. You wait too long to fight, do maybe one fight per year. It is what it is. I don't think it's the right way to do things."

Makhachev wanted Prates and Morales to fight to see who truly is the No. 1 contender. He admitted the winner will be one of the last fights of his career.

"Why is Makhachev talking about retirement? Maybe he made enough money and just wants to enjoy time with his family, in his own country, take care of his family," Prates said. "That's what everybody should do. At some point, you stop and take care of family, health and everything. I think he's doing the right thing."

If Makhachev isn't ready to go by summer, Prates hopes he doesn't hold up the division for too much longer.

"He should vacate his belt – not now. It's OK – we're going to fight for the interim belt," Prates said. "But after that, after Ramadan, we're planning to fight in June or something like that, and if he says, 'Oh, I'm not ready,' come on. Stop. Time to retire. Is June the deadline? Yeah."

Morales is undefeated, but Prates enters on three straight stoppage wins against top-level competition.

"I'm going to beat Morales," Prates said. "Nothing against him, nothing personal against him, just business. But I'm going to hurt him, I'm going to knock him out, and then I'm going to be really excited to fight Makhachev."

The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2735. Three reasons the Jaguars beat the Ravens

The Jacksonville Jaguars continued their impressive 2026 campaign on Thursday night, dismantling the Baltimore Ravens 33-10 at M&T Bank Stadium. In a game played through torrential rain, Trevor Lawrence and the offense did enough to put points on the board, but it was another outstanding defensive performance that ultimately made the difference.

Jacksonville improved to 6-2, extending its lead at the top of the AFC South, while Baltimore suffered a fourth consecutive defeat. There were plenty of reasons for optimism in another convincing Jaguars victory, but these three stood out.

Jacksonville's defense has quietly become one of the most reliable units in the NFL, and Thursday night provided another demonstration of just how good this group can be.

The Jaguars entered Week 9 ranked second in the NFL in points allowed, and they backed that reputation up by limiting Baltimore to just 227 total yards, 10 first downs and 10 points. The Ravens converted just four of their 14 third-down opportunities, while Jacksonville forced three turnovers, including interceptions by Montaric Brown and Jourdan Lewis.

Brown's interception came on Baltimore's opening possession of the second half, immediately putting the Jaguars in position to extend their lead. Lewis provided another takeaway in the fourth quarter, with both interceptions ultimately helping Jacksonville add field goals.

There was also an important battle in the trenches. Despite losing defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton for the season earlier in the week, Jacksonville restricted Derrick Henry to just 57 yards on 17 carries. That's an average of 3.4 yards per attempt against one of the most productive running backs of his generation.

Admittedly, Justice Hill's 65-yard touchdown run late in the fourth quarter took some of the shine off the final defensive numbers. However, until that point, Baltimore had managed just three points on its opening drive before going scoreless across its next nine offensive possessions.

The Ravens were missing Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley, but that shouldn't detract from the execution. Jacksonville did exactly what a good defense should do against a struggling offense: create pressure, take the football away and prevent the opposition from building any momentum.

This was another performance that suggests the Jaguars' defense can be a genuine strength as the season progresses.

Trevor Lawrence didn't need to put together a spectacular statistical performance to make his mark on this game. Instead, he delivered when Jacksonville needed him most.

The quarterback completed 16 of 26 passes for 242 yards and a touchdown, finishing with a 105.0 passer rating and spreading the football around eight different receivers.

His most important contribution came just before halftime. With the Jaguars holding a narrow 10-3 advantage, Lawrence led a four-play, 80-yard scoring drive that completely changed the complexion of the contest. The highlight was a beautifully executed 50-yard touchdown connection with Parker Washington, who beat his defender and found plenty of space behind the Baltimore secondary.

It was a significant moment. Jacksonville went into the locker room with a 17-3 lead rather than allowing the Ravens an opportunity to remain within one score and potentially build some momentum after the break.

Lawrence was particularly effective attacking downfield. According to Next Gen Stats, he completed eight of 10 passes travelling at least 10 air yards, accumulating 193 yards and a touchdown on those attempts. His 80% completion rate on downfield throws was his second-best mark of the season.

That's an encouraging development for a quarterback who has increasingly looked comfortable leading this offense.

There was no need for Lawrence to chase huge numbers in the second half. Jacksonville had established control, and he managed the game effectively while allowing the defense and special teams to do their jobs.

The Jaguars are becoming increasingly difficult to beat when their quarterback can produce big plays without needing to force the issue.

Perhaps the most encouraging aspect of this victory was how effectively Jacksonville's different units worked together.

This wasn't a game in which Lawrence needed to throw for 350 yards or the defense needed to score a touchdown to rescue the offense. Instead, the Jaguars consistently put themselves in advantageous positions and took the opportunities presented to them.

Their opening drive was an excellent example. Lawrence connected with tight end Nate Boerkircher for a 52-yard gain on the second play from scrimmage, setting up Bhayshul Tuten's one-yard touchdown run to give Jacksonville an early advantage.

The offense continued to find ways to move the football, while Cam Little converted all four of his field-goal attempts. Jacksonville finished with 319 total yards, averaging 5.7 yards per play, and produced seven scoring drives.

Importantly, the defense repeatedly helped the offense maintain control. Brown's interception set up a field goal early in the second half, while Lewis' fourth-quarter pick provided another short field. A fumble recovery by linebacker Jalen McLeod following the ensuing kickoff also helped Jacksonville put the game beyond doubt, with Chris Rodriguez Jr. eventually powering in from two yards out to make it 33-3.

It was a thoroughly professional performance in difficult conditions. The rain made life challenging for both offenses, but Jacksonville avoided the costly mistakes that could have allowed Baltimore back into the contest.

The Jaguars didn't need to dominate one particular statistical category to win. They simply executed their assignments, capitalized on mistakes and made sure the Ravens had very few opportunities to change the game's direction.

That's the kind of football that wins games in November and December.

There will be tougher tests ahead, and Jacksonville will need to maintain this level of performance against healthier and more dangerous opponents. However, back-to-back victories over the Indianapolis Colts and Baltimore Ravens have provided plenty of evidence that this team deserves to be taken seriously.

Lawrence is playing some of the best football of his career, the defense is consistently producing results, and the supporting cast is doing its part.

At 6-2, the Jaguars are building a significant cushion in the AFC South. More importantly, they're beginning to look like a team capable of making some serious noise when the postseason arrives.

#2734. Trinity Rodman, Sophia Wilson go head-to-head in NWSL playoff quarterfinal

Decision Day is in the rearview mirror and the 2026 NWSL playoffs start this weekend.

The quarterfinals kick off Friday and conclude on Sunday, Nov. 8, with a marquee matchup featuring Trinity Rodman and the Washington Spirit going head-to-head with Sophia Wilson and the Portland Thorns. The Spirit last won a championship in 2021, while the Thorns have won three overall, most recently in 2022.

Gotham FC are vying to become the first back-to-back champion since North Carolina Courage won consecutive titles in 2018-19, while the Utah Royals are set to make its first playoff appearance

Here's what you need to know ahead of the 2026 NWSL postseason:

2024: Orlando Pride (defeated Washington Spirit in the 2024 NWSL Championship game)

2013: Portland Thorns FC (defeated Western New York Flash in the championship game)

2024: Orlando Pride (defeated Washington Spirit in the 2024 NWSL Championship game)

2013: Portland Thorns FC (defeated Western New York Flash in the championship game)

Friday, Nov. 6 | 10 p.m. ET (Prime Video) | Snapdragon Stadium (San Diego)

For the first time in franchise history, the Utah Royals qualified for NWSL postseason. The Royals will lean heavily on Canadian forward Cloé Lacasse, who has done a little bit of everything this season, scoring eight goals and 10 assists to help Utah reach a franchise-best 14 wins. However, the Royals' dangerous offense enters the playoffs on a scoring drought that's stretched to 270 consecutive minutes entering the playoffs. Look for Lacasse, as well as Mina Tanaka (nine goals and five assists) to find the back of the net if the Royals want to take their historic run a step further and notch their first playoff win.

San Diego is riding a wave of momentum as the club makes its first postseason appearance since 2023. The Wave have won eight of their last 10 and set single-season records for wins (18) and points (58). Trinity Byars recorded a team-high 14 contributions for the Wave this season, becoming the second player in club history to record double-digit goals in a single season with 11 goals and three assists. Alex Morgan was the first with 15 goals in 2022. Melanie Barcena, 19, added a career-high seven goals and three assists.

The Wave has defeated Utah every time they've faced off since the Royals returned to the league in 2024, with San Diego boasting a 6-0 all-time record against Utah, including both matchups between the teams this season.

Saturday, Nov. 7 | 12 p.m. ET (CBS/Paramount+) | CPKC Stadium (Kansas City)

After recording the winningest regular season in NWSL history last year, Kansas City came down to earth with a 16-win season under first-year coach Chris Armas. The Current finished with 54 goals, tying Angel City FC with the most in the league. The high-scoring offenses will go head-to-head on Saturday.

The Current enter the matchup on five-match winning streak, led by forwards Temwa Chawinga and Haley Hopkins, who each have scored 12 goals a piece this season. Midfielder Croix Bethune, who was acquired from the Washington Spirit in a $1 million transfer in February, led the league with 11 assists, including six game-winning assists, to set a new NWSL single-season record.

Angel City enters the postseason on a 10-game unbeaten streak after recording club single-season records for points (52) and wins (15). Sveindís Jane Jónsdóttir broke Angel City's single-season record with 10 goals this season. Angel City won the first matchup between the teams, 2-1, while the second matchup of the season resulted in a 1-1 draw.

Sunday, Nov. 8 | 12:30 p.m. ET (ABC) | Sports Illustrated Stadium (New Jersey)

Gotham FC has flipped the script. The club entered the 2025 postseason as the No. 8 seed and went on to become the lowest seed to win an NWSL championship in league history. This year, Gotham FC enters the playoffs as the No. 1 seed after winning the club's first NWSL Shield, which is awarded to the team with the most points at the end of the regular-season. The firsts didn't stop there. The defending champions set club records in wins (18), points (61) and shutouts (14) as they look to win their third title in four seasons.

"It's definitely a historic day for the club," Gotham FC coach Juan Carlos Amorós said. "At least for a week, we are champions of the NWSL Championship, champions of the NWSL Challenge Cup, and now we are champions of the NWSL Shield, which means that basically we're winners of everything, and we're going to try to win the championship again."

Jaedyn Shaw will be key to Gotham FC's title defense. Shaw has a team-high 16 contributions with 11 goals and six assists. Esther González, Gotham's all-time top scorer, scored six goals this season to extend her own record.

Meanwhile, the Reign are looking to end Jess Fishlock's NWSL career on a high note after claiming the last spot in the 2026 NWSL playoffs. Fishlock, who joined the Reign in the league's inaugural season in 2013, is set to retire at the conclusion of the season. The 39-year-old brings leadership to the youthful team, in addition to the four goals and one assist she recorded this season to surpass Megan Rapinoe as the Reign's all-time leading scorer. Forward/midfielder Maddie Mercado has a team-high 10 goals.

"I've said it before and I'll say it again. This group … the only sad thing about my retirement is I don't get more time with them," Fishlock said. "I would love to spend another couple of years just being a part of their growth and them reaching what they want to reach, because I love them. I do."

Sunday, Nov. 8 | 3 p.m. ET (ABC) | Audi Field (Washington DC)

The final quarterfinal match of the weekend features heavyweights USWNT teammates Trinity Rodman and Sophia Wilson, who won Olympic gold together at the 2024 Paris Olympics. On Sunday, they're rivals.

Both are in midst of career years. Wilson scored a career-best 15 goals and five assists in 28 games in her first season back from maternity leave after giving birth to daughter Gianna in September 2025. That figure could be even higher had Wilson not served a two-game suspension following a red card for hair pulling. Wilson enters Sunday's playoff matchup red-hot after recording a brace in the Thorns regular-season finale.

Rodman turned in the most productive season of her career, with highs in goals (12), assists (8) and games (30). She'll look to lead the Spirit over the hump after the club was defeated in the championship game the past two seasons. The 2026 NWSL championship will be held at Audi Field on Nov. 21. Is third time the charm?

#2733. 6 cooked NBA teams already serving up a lost season

The NBA's 82-game regular season leaves plenty of margin for error for a bad stretch of play. This is a league where 53% of teams make the playoffs, not counting the four other teams who have the opportunity to earn their way into the postseason with one or two wins in the play-in tournament. There are still five months left on the schedule, with back-to-backs and spells of three-games-in-four-nights filling in the calendar.

Most teams can get off to a bad start and still be just fine. Some teams already know their season is over before it ever really starts. Check out our NBA power rankings this week for full coverage of the league.

Just over two weeks into the season, it already feels like there are six teams who are already toast. Some of these teams knew they would be bad coming into the year, while others dreamed of breaking into the playoffs. The unfortunate reality for these teams is they can't even count on a high draft pick next year anymore after the league's anti-tanking lottery reform was put in place this season ahead of the 2027 draft. Of course, there's plenty of time for things to change with only about 10% of the schedule complete, but these six teams already look cooked.

The Kings appeared to have no hope coming into the season, and at this point the only intrigue left is to see if they avoid being the worst team of the 2020s, a stake currently held by the 14-win Detroit Pistons in 2023-24. Rookie guard Darius Acuff is the best thing this franchise has going for them, and he's getting thrown into the deep end from the very start of his career. Acuff leads the NBA in minutes per game and he's one field goal attempt behind 2-time MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander for the league-lead in that category. The Kings could probably stand to give some of Acuff's usage (32.5%) to Domantas Sabonis (16.1% usage rate), but they would still be a bad team, and at least now the rookie guard has the ability to learn from his mistakes. Keegan Murray being out again with an ankle injury after only playing 23 games last year is the real bummer for the start of this season. The Kings felt like the worst team in the league entering the season, and they still feel like the worst team in the league. Try to enjoy the Acuff roller coaster, Kings fans, because there's nothing else to latch onto.

The good news is that rookie forward Caleb Wilson looks like he can be the franchise player the Bulls have been missing since their horrible Jimmy Butler trade 10 years ago. The bad news is they might need four new starters around him long-term. It's been a truly disappointing start for Matas Buzelis, who looked like a keeper in his first two seasons under Billy Donovan, but is regressing and seemingly falling out of favor under new head coach Tiago Splitter. Buzelis' inability to beat mismatches when teams put their tiny guards on him is the single most alarming trend of this season for Chicago. Josh Giddey has also been terrible, and likely won't be around the next time the Bulls have a playoff team. No. 15 overall pick Dailyn Swain can't even get on the floor during blowouts. Chicago's perimeter defense is atrocious with Giddey and Norm Powell, it can't grab a defensive rebound (No. 28 in d-rebound rate), and it's dead-last in three-point percentage. This team stinks out loud, but a brutal schedule to open the season will get softer eventually, and Wilson's highlights will at least give the fanbase something to dream on.

It was simply unavoidable that the Bucks would be in for a hard season after trading Giannis Antetokounmpo, and it's playing out as expected. Milwaukee is hanging tough in most of their games under new head coach Taylor Jenkins, but they just don't have the talent to win in the fourth quarter yet. Milwaukee is dead-last at forcing turnovers on defense, and they're near the bottom of the league in both free throw rate and free throw percentage. The Bucks just don't get anything easy right now, which is the true sign of a terrible team. There are some positives thus far: rookie guard Brayden Burries looks pretty good despite a cold start as a shooter, while Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Tyler Herro are both playing well enough to fetch something decent on the trade market. Kel'el Ware, who is playing under 19 minutes per game, has possibly been the biggest disappointment here so far with a lot of sloppy turnovers, undisciplined fouls, and bricked jumpers to start the year. Getting Ware going next to Burries would at least improve the vibes the rest of the way.

The Suns became the feel-good story of last season by grinding out 45 wins with maximum effort on the offensive glass and forcing defensive takeaways. This year's team had to take a step forward after trading their last remaining future first-round pick for Miles Bridges, but it was easy to tell that move was doomed to fail from the start. Bridges hasn't added much of anything to Phoenix at either end of the floor, but that's just the start of their problems. This team continues to play Jalen Green over Collin Gillespie for some reason, even though every piece of evidence points to Gillespie being the exact player they need. The Suns have more of a chance to turn it around this season than most of these other teams provided they finally start playing their best point guard, but their issues in the middle don't have such an easy solution. I loved Khaman Maluach as a draft prospect, but he just doesn't look ready for starting center minutes at all right now. Oso Ighodaro has been better offensively, but he's too small to play full-time center, and the defense completely falls apart when he's on the floor (a ghastly 129 defensive rating in his minutes). Devin Booker is getting paid enough to lift this team through tough times, but he's just not a great enough shot-maker to overcome his lack of rim attempts. Phoenix has some chance to turn it around, but the early returns are highly discouraging.

I was foolish enough to think the Jazz could be a playoff team this year, but my optimism started to fade once Jusuf Nurkic went down with a foot injury in the team's preseason opener. A length injury to Jaren Jackson Jr. followed, which has put an already thin front court in a dangerous spot to start the season. It's a bad sign that Utah's offense has been the main culprit for their struggles, ranking No. 29 in the league right now. There should be a ton of firepower here, but the team has been ice cold from three (31.5 percent, No. 27 in the league), and rookie Darryn Peterson is still figuring out his spots on the floor. Peterson is relying way too heavily on floaters and other non-rim two-pointers right now, and it's tanking his efficiency (46.5% true shooting). There's also just a huge lack of high-level passing on this team right now, and it's one reason why Lauri Markkanen just can't seem to get going. The JJJ trade looks like an abomination. This was supposed to be the season the Jazz finally stopped rebuilding and started getting serious, but the product on the floor remains extremely poor.

The Clippers' future was decimated by the NBA for their dealings with Kawhi Leonard in a cap circumvention scandal, but they still had a chance to be competitive this year. It already feels like that hope is over. Brandon Ingram reported to training camp with a partially torn Achilles, Max Strus is just returning now from a foot injury, and the big man room might be the worst in the league. Meanwhile, Darius Garland is turning the ball over like crazy, and rookie Keaton Wagler might be the worst inside the arc scorer in the NBA (25% on two-pointers). The Clippers turn the ball over more than any team in the league, and only four clubs allow their opponents to score with better efficiency. Worst of all, they owe their 2027 draft pick to the Thunder. I have mad respect for Ty Lue as a head coach, but there's nothing he can do to stop this mess.

#2732. New Bayern deal makes Kane Europe's best-paid player

After several rounds of negotiations, Bayern Munich finally announced on Thursday that Harry Kane had signed a new contract running until 2029.

According to Sky Germany and AZ, Kane will earn a club-record salary, surpassing his previous €25 million per year.

The new deal is the most lucrative in Bayern's history, with sources telling The Athletic's David Ornstein that the 33-year-old is now the highest-paid player in European football in terms of guaranteed salary, although some players are thought to be able to earn more overall when bonuses are included.

Ornstein also reports that, despite Kane now being 33, Bayern don't see this as his final contract with the club.

According to AZ, Bayern CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen held eight rounds of negotiations with the striker's father and brother before finally getting the deal over the line.

Kane and his representatives reportedly wanted a contract until 2030, or at least an option to extend the deal until then. However, according to AZ, the final agreement doesn't include such an option.

In return, Bayern made concessions to the striker in other areas, including his salary and image rights.

#2727. 5 things to watch as Jets face Chiefs in Week 8 of 2026 NFL season

The Jets have fallen to 2-6 on the season and will be looking back on the last few games with regret as matchups they will feel they should have won.

It's a different proposition this week, though, as they will be heavy underdogs in their visit to face the Kansas City Chiefs.

Let's review the top storylines to watch as the Jets look to pull off the upset...

The Chiefs got off to a 5-0 start but have since lost their last two. Clearly, they'll be expecting to halt that slide on Sunday.

Unfortunately for New York, the two-game losing streak makes it unlikely the Chiefs overlook them. It will be a good measuring stick for the Jets, who have suffered five of their six losses this season in one-score games.

Defensive linemen David Onyemata and T'Vondre Sweat are already on IR, and now Harrison Phillips has an injury concern after an ankle issue kept him out of practice on Wednesday. If Phillips is unable to play on Sunday, the Jets will be without all three of their starting linemen.

That bodes well for the Chiefs, who have the No. 5 rushing game in the NFL. Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker, who was signed during the offseason, is just 10 yards off the league lead with 770.

Last Sunday, to their credit, the Jets did quite well against the run, as they held the Raiders below three yards per carry. Backups Darrell Jackson Jr., Jowon Briggs and Jack Heflin will need to continue to hold their own, even if Phillips suits up.

It's been a long time since the Jets had as many offensive weapons at their disposal as they do right now. However, they are still striving for the right balance in terms of getting everyone involved.

Last week saw New York make an effort to involve Garrett Wilson more, and featured a career-high 142-yard game from AD Mitchell, who had gone without a catch in the previous game. However, Omar Cooper Jr. wasn't targeted at all coming off back-to-back 100-yard games and the team drew criticism for abandoning the running game in the second half.

This has been an issue all year. After a breakout 100-yard game against the Lions, rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq has just five catches for 43 yards in the past five weeks. In addition, Jeremy Ruckert – who had a career-high five catches and a touchdown in the same game – hasn't been targeted at all since then.

Having been outstanding in 2025, the Jets' special teams unit has been poor in 2026, and it let them down again on Sunday when Dylan Laube returned a kickoff for a 95-yard touchdown. Can Chris Banjo's unit use this game to get back to the kind of impact they were making last season?

One area where the Jets might have the edge is in the kicking game, because the usually stellar Harrison Butker has really been struggling. Butker has missed six field goals, and his 67 percent success rate this season is easily the lowest of his career. Butker will be feeling the pressure to be flawless on Sunday after the Chiefs recently added Justin Tucker to their practice squad as competition for him.

Back in Week 4, Minkah Fitzpatrick's interception of Tyson Bagent snapped New York's incredible streak of 21 games without an interception. In addition, they intercepted another three passes that day, although each of those was negated by a penalty. Nevertheless, it seemed like a strong sign that this year's team would be much better at making plays on the ball.

Since then, however, four games have passed and the Jets have failed to intercept a pass in any of them. Including Fitzpatrick's interception, the Jets have just one in 25 games under Glenn, as that play is starting to look more like an aberration than a sign this would start becoming a more regular occurrence.

#2726. Boyne City volleyball has to dig deep for D3 district title over Charlevoix

CHARLEVOIX — There was no scenario where the Boyne City volleyball team would exit Charlevoix without a challenge from the host Rayders Thursday night.

It was the first time the Ramblers were meeting their heated rival in the postseason since 2016 and first time since 2013 that the two were playing for a title.

So, despite a regular season sweep, a challenge is exactly what the Ramblers got in their Division 3 district championship match.

"They made us work for every last point and this match could have gone either way," Boyne City coach Shannon Flippin said.

The Ramblers had to grind through two opening sets, dropped the third, then found a way to close the door in the fourth for the title.

In Flippin's eyes, it took everyone involved.

"Our team, our student section, and our friends and family really all combined for this win," he said. "Without their support this could have been much different."

Petoskey District Title: Unique blend of Petoskey volleyball players capture D1 district title

PHS Title Photos: See Petoskey volleyball celebrate its Division 1 district championship

Boyne City picked up wins of 25-21 and 25-22 in the first two sets, then dropped a 25-15 match.

"We played tough the first two sets and then stopped putting pressure on them in the third set and they took advantage in a big way," Flippin said.

In that third set, Flippin talked with his team late during a timeout about the importance of staying aggressive. From that moment on, Boyne was on the attack, led by Maitlyn Barkley on the outside.

Barkley finished that third set loss with three kills, then the Ramblers carried that late-set momentum into the fourth to earn a 25-18 win and 3-1 victory.

"Our play to win mentality helped us pull away towards the end of that set," Flippin added.

East Jordan-Boyne Falls: Top photos from East Jordan's district title victory over Boyne Falls

EJ Final Point: East Jordan volleyball secures final point for district championship

Charlevoix closed out a 27-19-4 season with the defeat. It was a season that came with a midseason coaching change and a key injury late in the season for a relatively young Rayder team still.

Charlevoix graduates the likes of Addison Shearer, Jaslyn Blanton, Victoria Carroll, Ayla Kemp, Taryn Carey and Olive Grossi, with Kemp a four-year varsity player and Blanton, Shearer and Carey all three-year members.

Boyne's Addy Burns: Addy Burns helping Boyne City volleyball keep wind in its sails

The district championship for the Ramblers comes as their first at the Division 3 level since topping Charlevoix in 2013 and now they'll get the same exact regional opponent from that season ahead.

Boyne will next head to an Elk Rapids hosted Division 3 regional semifinal at 6 p.m., Tuesday, Nov. 10 against Traverse City St. Francis (29-17-2).

Between conference, tournament and district play at the end of the season, Boyne City is now on an 11-1 stretch over their last 12 games, having built a now 25-18-3 record.

Once an old league rival, the Ramblers and Glads have not met this season. St. Francis advanced through its district with a four-set victory over Elk Rapids in the district final.

Match stats were not available for both teams as of Friday morning. Check back with the News-Review.

#2725. Three reasons why the Brewers can repeat as World Series champions in 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers are the freshly crowned World Series champions for 2026. Add that trophy to a regular season body of work in which they won 103 games and achieved the best run differential in all of Major League Baseball, and it's clear the Brewers this season did all a team can do. The first title in franchise history will be remembered and cherished by the Brewers and their fans forever, and it was earned in every respect.

The celebrations won't soon end, and the post-Game 5 hangovers are still pulsing. Even so, it's time to turn our attention to the 2027 season and explore why the Brewers absolutely have the foundation necessary to do it all again next year. Here, then, are three reasons the Brewers can become repeat champions roughly one year from now.

Eyeball the Brewers' current contract obligations and service time tiers, and you'll find just six players are likely bound for free agency. Brandon Woodruff, Jake Bauers, JoJo Romero, and Gary Sánchez will be free agents soon. Elsewhere, Dustin May has a mutual option for 2027, which means he'll probably join them. Finally, Antonio Senzatela has a $14 million team option for 2027 on which the Brewers may pass.

Of those, the 31-year-old Bauers is the biggest needle-mover, as he's coming off a 2026 season in which he hit 26 home runs in 144 games and put up a WAR of 3.3. He does seem likely to move on, but the Brewers are more than resourceful enough to find comparable production from the non-premium position of first base.

Elsewhere, the Brewers should resist the temptation to trade away catcher, linchpin, and reigning World Series MVP William Contreras ahead of his walk year in 2027. The Brewers Way in recent years has been to part ways with core contributors around such a time, and that may be a temptation with Contreras, especially given Bo Naylor's presence on the roster. Contreras, though, is not easily replaceable given his skills behind the mask and his high level of production at the plate. An extension may not be something the Brewers will pursue – even though the ongoing CBA negotiations will probably lead to a new system that benefits teams like Milwaukee – but even if that's the case, they should keep their catcher and leader around for the final year of team control in the name of defending the belt and the title.

The champion Brewers, as a club that gets limited investment from ownership and is elite at player development, skews young even as they stand as the best team in baseball. Consider:

As for specific examples, they're not hard to find. Budding star Jackson Chourio will be in his age-23 campaign in 2027. Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson will each be 25. Cooper Pratt, like Chourio, will be 23. The Brewers this past season got 16.4 WAR from those names, and Pratt and Henderson didn't even log full seasons.

Let's also note that Brice Turang, who led the Brewers this season with a WAR of 7.3, will be just 27 in '27 and thus should continue performing at a high level. This isn't just a matter of the Brewers being largely shielded from age-related decline next season. There's also the distinct possibility that so many of their 2026 pace-setters are still pre-prime and may have even better days ahead.

As though all of the above weren't enough, the Brewers right now have managed to thread this rare needle: they're the best team at the highest level and have one of the best collections of talent down on the farm. MLB.com in August ranked the Brewers as the third-best farm system in the game right now. FanGraphs ranked them third based on average prospect value. Baseball America at midseason likewise ranked the Milwaukee system third and after the season gave the system an "A" grade.

At an individual level, a number of premium Brewers prospects figure to arrive at some point next season. That list includes shortstop Jesús Made, who may be the top prospect in the game right now. Other 2027 arrivals may include talents like corner infielder Andrew Fischer, right-handers Tyson Hardin and Bishop Letson, and infielder/outfielder Jett Williams, among others. So many teams in contending mode have a fairly dry pipeline thanks to the low draft picks and the now-for-later trades that often accompany World Series aspirations, but that's very much not the case with lead executive Matt Arnold and the Brewers.

Celebrations of the work done in 2026 should be the focus right now for the Crew and their rooters, and once that dies down, they can all be further buoyed by the reality that the Brewers aren't going anywhere. The guess here is that the Brewers open the 2027 season – whatever it looks like — as the consensus favorites to do it all again.

Wisconsin Ave. in downtown Milwaukee and ending at Henry Maier Festival ParkWhen: Starting at 10 a.m. CST on Friday, Oct. 30Cost: The parade is free and open to the publicTV/streaming: Nationally on MLB Network, MLB.tv, Brewers.tv, and Brewers.com (fuboTV, try for free); locally on CBS 58 starting at 9 a.m. CST.

The rally at Henry Maier Festival Park opens at 8 a.m. and will include large video screens featuring live parade coverage, live music, food and beverage offerings, exclusive merchandise and more. Brewers alumni will also be in attendance and the first 50,000 fans at the rally will receive a limited-edition championship rally towel.

🏆 Milwaukee, the celebration continues!Join the @Brewers for the Parade of Champions tomorrow, Friday, Oct. 30! 💙💛Starts at 10 AM at N. 4th St. & W. Wisconsin Ave., ending at Summerfest grounds for the Championship Rally!Full details: https://t.co/0r5qC7R61X pic.twitter.com/9CQJmK9Vzz

Milwaukee Public Schools also announced that school will be canceled for all students and staff on Friday for the parade and celebration.

Given the enthusiasm shown by Brewers fans throughout this season and especially the playoffs – they may have been the majority presence in Game 5 at Tropicana Field – it no doubt will be an enthusiastic and memorable celebration. Brewers supporters, after all, have been waiting 57 years for just such an event.
