#2692. Organized Chaos: Bournemouth’s Possession Principles Against Nottingham – MH

von Next Generation am 28.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League,Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

On Matchday 23, the two surprise teams of the Premier League faced off. Nottingham, unbeaten in their last nine matches, has impressed this season with outstanding defensive work. Bournemouth, coached by Andoni Iraola and now unbeaten in 12 games, takes a completely different tactical approach compared to most other teams. In an interview with TNT Sports, Guardiola remarked: “Today, modern football is the way Bournemouth, Newcastle, Brighton, and Liverpool play.” What exactly are these teams doing differently? Bournemouth’s approach will be analyzed in detail based on this match.

Bournemouth’s coach, Andoni Iraola, is a former player under Marcelo Bielsa at Athletic Bilbao. Bielsa, widely known in the Premier League as the coach who led Leeds United to promotion, gained recognition for his style of play characterized by exceptionally high intensity in all phases of the game. According to Iraola, his own footballing philosophy has been significantly shaped by his former coach Bielsa.

In an interview with Sky, back when he was still managing Rayo Vallecano, Iraola stated: “I was very lucky to play for him (Bielsa) for two seasons as a player. I think he has another vision of football. They were two very good seasons for us, and, for me, it was a different knowledge.” He also explained: “I use a lot of exercises from Marcelo that I learned from him. I use a lot of things, especially with the ball. Offensively, his teams are very dynamic. He is willing to make all the runs to the space, he is ready to accept this kind of disorder, offensively.”

Iraola’s tactical concept can be described as “organized chaos.” The aim is not to implement a positional system with perfect patterns of play. Instead, the focus is on creating problems for opposing teams by generating chaos. The idea is to force the opponent into unfamiliar, uncontrolled phases of play. A particularly important concept within this is highly intense, man-oriented, hybrid attacking pressing, designed to force the opponent into quick turnovers and a fast-paced, direct game.

„It is true that we like, and we perform better, in high-tempo games. We need to run a lot. We don’t need so much control, not in every single play, but I think we have the legs, we have the willingness, to go up and down.“ – Iraola

Accordingly, Iraola’s style of play could face challenges against deep-lying teams that deliberately thrive on minimal possession. These teams don’t need to engage with Bournemouth’s high-intensity game but can instead remain compact out of possession. They are not required to build up play from the back under Bournemouth’s pressing to maintain controlled possession but can focus on their own offensive transitions. This season, Nottingham has been one of the most successful teams in executing such an approach. Consequently, it was particularly intriguing to observe how Iraola’s Bournemouth would operate in possession against Nottingham’s deep block.

Iraola describes his philosophy in possession as follows:

“We have to prepare [positional] patterns, but we cannot just prioritise them. If you can see that you don’t have a teammate ahead, forget about the pattern, just drive the ball and try to force things to happen. I want him to attack first.”

Here lies the challenge I encountered while analyzing the game against Nottingham: how do you describe intentionally provoked chaos, where there are barely any fixed patterns? Only a few predefined sequences can be identified within the positional framework. The crucial question, therefore, is: what reference points structure Bournemouth’s possession play, and which principles of play create this chaos? Or, put simply: what “tools” does Iraola use in his style of play? To answer this, the positional framework of the game against Nottingham will first be examined.

Starting from a nominal 4-2-3-1 formation, Nottingham defended out of possession in a 4-4-1-1 or 4-5-1 structure. Nottingham focused primarily on defending and largely conceded possession to Bournemouth, a characteristic approach for the team. Under coach Simoes Espirito Santo, Nottingham has averaged just 40% possession this season.

Bournemouth, meanwhile, operated in possession with a positional 2-4-4 or 2-3-2-3 structure, featuring wide wingers and full-backs. From this setup, Bournemouth attempted to break through Nottingham’s deep block. On the (left) No. 10 position, Kluivert stood out with his exceptional dribbling ability and high agility. Central midfielder Christie alternated between the deeper right half-space as a right-sided No. 10 and the No. 6 position.

Nottingham was often forced back into their own half from an initially higher defensive pressing. When Nottingham attempted to press higher, Bournemouth’s center-backs positioned themselves wide, and goalkeeper Kepa moved up to form part of the back line. This made it nearly impossible for Nottingham’s lone striker to put significant pressure on the ball carrier. As a result, Nottingham dropped deep, retreated, and refrained from pressing the ball-carrying center-backs.

„I sometimes value much more a player carrying the ball and forcing things to happen. I think when you play too positional – one, two touches to find a free man – you sometimes lose the initiative from the players to just take their man on and attack the spaces.” – Iraola

This approach meant that Bournemouth’s center-backs were frequently required to dribble forward against stationary opponents, forcing defenders to commit. This often created 5v4 or 4v4 situations on the flanks, caused by the strong lateral movements of striker Ouattara and attacking midfielder Kluivert, combined with the forward dribbling of the center-backs. When no passingoptions were available, the team didn’t rebuild play, as is typical for positionally oriented teams. Instead, Bournemouth’s left center-back, Huijsen, was occasionally seen dribbling directly at the opponent’s last defensive line. It can be concluded that one of Iraola’s key principles of play is to attack vertically with the ball as early as possible.

Center-back Huijsen dribbles toward the final defensive line himself due to a lack of better-positioned deeper passing options.

The situations on the flanks during the center-back’s dribbling were played out in various ways. Sometimes the ball was passed to the wide player on the wing, who was tasked with taking on a 1v1 duel. This player was consistently supported by the full-back in a dual-width setup.

Particularly noteworthy were the positional rotations of the 3-4 players on the flanks. Full-backs, attacking midfielder Kluivert, striker Ouattara, and the winger frequently rotated out of their positions, occupying different spaces. What stood out was the consistent presence of a dynamic deep run within these rotations, forcing the opponent to cover the run and thereby creating space between their players.

The positional rotations with deep runs create passing options.

For example, the left-back Kerkez, during the center-back’s dribble, occasionally made deep runs into the half-space. Similarly, attacking midfielder Kluivert was often involved, sometimes shifting laterally to receive the ball and then driving forward at pace to attack the defensive block.

Nottingham responded to this from the 30th minute by attempting to apply more pressure on Bournemouth’s ball-carrying center-backs. The 4-4-1-1 shape was adjusted by removing the man-marking on defensive midfielder Adams. Instead, Nottingham transitioned into a 4-4-2 setup, aiming to position Adams in the cover shadow and step out earlier to press the center-backs. However, Bournemouth’s goalkeeper Kepa played so high in the back line that he was still able to connect with the now even wider-positioned center-backs, allowing them to continue dribbling forward.

The goalkeeper stepping into the back line creates a 4v2 situation, allowing the center-backs to dribble forward with less pressure from opponents.

“I would say they have the freedom to risk a little bit in the dribbles.“ – Iraola

Another key principle of Bournemouth’s possession game is diagonal, vertical dribbling. These serve as a chaos factor and are constantly utilized across all positions. As long as no teammate is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal, players are given the freedom to dribble. The skillful dribblers on the wings, the striker, and attacking midfielder Kluivert fit perfectly into this principle. The spaces opened up through the aforementioned rotations, particularly between the opposing players on the flanks, were mostly attacked through dribbling rather than passing.

The core idea behind this focus on dribbling is closely aligned with the concept of relationism. The goal is to make the team’s decisions less predictable for the opponent and to create a certain degree of chaos. Traditional positional play often limits players’ individual freedom, which reduces the element of surprise. However, Iraola’s execution of possession football differs significantly from relationism.

Instead of using a tighter structure to encourage combinations between players, rotations and larger distances between players are used to create spaces intended to be attacked through dribbling. It is crucial that these dribbles are always executed as vertical actions, continually putting the opponent under defensive pressure and thereby opening up other options.

Due to the larger spaces on the flanks, many dribbles are initiated on the wing, supported by the dual-width occupation of the winger and full-back. To enforce a successful follow-up action against deep-lying opponents, proper box occupation is a fundamental requirement. Iraola’s teams often flood the opponent’s penalty area with up to seven players, forcing the opposition right in front of their own goal. The goal is not necessarily to find the open player but to increase the likelihood of winning the ball after a cross in the penalty area. Second balls also play a significant role in this approach.

Risky dribbles have the additional advantage of provoking more frequent transition moments. When the opponent tries to transition offensively, they lose their compact defensive shape. Bournemouth’s flexible rest defense allows the ball to be immediately recovered after a loss of possession. Bournemouth’s rest defense typically consists of 3-4 players, depending on the attacking structure. In addition to the two center-backs, defensive midfielder Adams and the inverted, far-side full-back provide cover. If both full-backs or Adams are involved in the attack, Christie drops deeper to provide support and shifts closer to the ball.

On one hand, it’s important to highlight the excellent sense of positioning from the two central midfielders, Adams and Christie, in anticipating potential turnovers. Their ability to read these moments and their spatial awareness lead to many successful counter-pressing actions. On the other hand, the immediate pressure applied to the ball-carrying opponent after a turnover is notable, leaving the opposition with little opportunity to create controlled possession phases.

As a result, Nottingham’s offensive presence in the first half was minimal. Successful offensive transitions by Simoes Espirito Santo’s team were extremely rare.

The rest-defense structure in the 21st minute consists of the inverted Kerkez, the shifting defensive midfielder Adams, and the center-backs. At the same time, the ball-near teammates position themselves in response to the dribble in a way that allows them to immediately apply pressure if needed.

Another key principle of Bournemouth’s play is that after regaining possession, the first action is immediately directed forward. In contrast to traditionally positional teams, control is not sought through possession in chaotic situations but rather through constant transitions. The goal is to prevent the opponent from regaining their structure and settling into their usual rhythm. This creates intense pressure for Bournemouth’s opponents. As a result, Bournemouth often didn’t even need to break down Nottingham’s defensive block because the opponent never had the chance to regain their typical structure.

After recovering the ball, Bournemouth consistently looked to play forward into pressure. When positioned deeper (closer to their own goal), players in the forward zones immediately made runs into space to create vertical passing options. Even if the Bournemouth player who regained the ball was immediately under pressure, the first action was directed forward.

If necessary, a long ball was played toward the opponent’s defensive line, with a focus on winning second balls. This pressing game with an emphasis on second balls—often referred to as “kick and rush”—generated additional forced transition situations, preventing the opponent from finding their usual shape. The fact that four of Bournemouth’s five goals against the typically deep-lying Nottingham team came from deliberately provoked transition moments highlights the effectiveness of this approach.

In the second half, Nottingham switched to an attacking press in an attempt to create more scoring opportunities and overturn the 1-0 deficit. However, Nottingham was unable to pin Bournemouth in their own half as planned. Instead, Bournemouth played targeted long balls to one of their four advanced attackers or to the half-high positioned full-backs. Through a combination of winning second balls, dribbles, and central midfielders following up for lay-offs, Bournemouth was able to quickly progress into space and control the game from their own half. This led to Bournemouth scoring their second and third goals in quick succession. The final result was a resounding 5-0 victory for Iraola’s side.

So, what exactly causes the chaos in Bournemouth’s possession play? In summary, it is a combination of the principles discussed: playing vertically as early as possible; dribbling diagonally and vertically as long as no player is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal; and making the first action after regaining possession a forward one. The focus on vertical zones (reference point: opponent players) and second balls (reference point: the opponent’s goal) creates an intense and dynamic style of play that prevents the opponent from settling into their usual structure. Bournemouth is further aided by their attacking press, which was not analyzed in detail in this article but consistently provokes additional transition situations.

What can other teams take away from Bournemouth’s possession approach without abandoning their own philosophy? One lesson is the courage to consistently seek depth, provided the team has appropriate counter-pressing structures in place. Additionally, the dynamism of individual actions at Bournemouth is remarkable. Rarely have I seen such explosive runs into depth from other teams.

The final question is: what do the teams mentioned by Guardiola in the aforementioned interview have in common? All of them attack the depth quickly and frequently, making the game incredibly dynamic and intense. This forces the opponent to make decisions faster. After all, the main difference between good and very good players is the time it takes to make a good decision.

My recommendation is to watch games from 30 years ago. It quickly becomes apparent that football has become faster and more demanding.

“For me, the players are better than in 2003. They have to do the same things, but much faster. The physical demands are ridiculous. I doubt I could have played at this rhythm.” – Iraola

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2691. Micah Parsons details why knee recovery has taken so long, refuses to set timeline for Packers return

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Green Bay Packers star Micah Parsons has been out since tearing his ACL during the Packers' Week 15 loss to the Denver Broncos last season. But there is some light at the end of the tunnel.

Parsons had his 21-day practice window open on Wednesday, so he spoke with local media for the first time about his injury and recovery process. However, there's still no set timeline on when he should return to the field. Even if there was, he likely wouldn't let us know.

"I just want it to be a surprise," Parsons said during his media availability regarding the timeline.  "I just want it to be a fulfilling moment for myself, the staff — just to enjoy that day and not put too much pressure on that day. My family [has] even been asking me, 'You going to play? Should we buy flights to come out there?'

"But I'm not going to pinpoint a day to disappoint anyone or give people expectations that I can't meet."

Parsons noted that in addition to having surgery on the torn ACL, he had a full repair of the medial and lateral menisci in his knee. He was therefore non-weight-bearing for two months, which is why his recovery timeline has been longer than some other players who have suffered torn ACLs in recent years.

Parsons said he had to undergo in-depth conditioning to get his body back into shape, just to get to the point he is right now. But there's still a long process ahead. He doesn't expect to be his full self when he does get back into game action.

"My conditioning right now is probably the worst it's been in my career," Parsons said. "And that's just the reality of it. Am I going to go out there and play 50, 60 snaps how I was doing before? Absolutely not. It's just not realistic. My body is not there yet...So I'm not going to be the All-Pro Micah, the person I once was, this year. Probably not until later, after I go through my phases and things like that, but I think what people will see is they'll see this guy is ready to play football. He's going to play hard, and he's going to boost this defense that's already doing a great job."

"I think those types of things you won't question, and I think you'll see flashes of All-Pro Micah when I do the pass rush, and there will be times where it's like, 'Dang, what was Micah doing?' And there's going to be times I question myself too...Because the reality is I just came back from an 11-month injury."

Even though Parsons has already been out for nearly a full year and will still take some more time to return to the field for actual games, he feels like he took the right course in his rehab process. He felt "the patience was absolutely worth it" and hopes to make a full run with the team well into December and into the playoffs.

Parsons is returning to a Packers team that has turned its season around over the last few weeks. Green Bay fell to 1-2 with an embarrassing "Thursday Night Football" loss to the Atlanta Falcons in late September but has since gone 4-1, with the lone loss coming by three points against the division rival Detroit Lions. As they head into the stretch run of the season, the Packers are in position to make a playoff push. And Parsons feels as though he is getting ready to return at the perfect moment.

"I came back for the greatest time of football," he said. "And that's November football and December football. Let the show begin."

#2690. Why Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell should be on hot seat despite NFL-best 6-1 record

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Minnesota Vikings (6-1) are in co-possession of the best record in the NFL with the Buffalo Bills and the San Francisco 49ers entering Week 9, the halfway point of the 2026 season. However, head coach Kevin O'Connell should be on the hot seat.

How could both of those things be true? Let's take a quick look at what is powering the Vikings' early-season success and then take a deep dive into why O'Connell's bungling of his quarterback position -- both in 2026 and years prior -- in tandem with wasting Justin Jefferson and a poor playoff record should be causing his seat to be increasing in temperature.

O'Connell is Minnesota's head coach and offensive play caller, but defensive coordinator Brian Flores' blitzkrieg defense is why the Vikings have won six of their first seven games. Minnesota's defense leads the NFL in the following statistics:

However, O'Connell's offense is powered by 2022 NFL Offensive Player of the Year wide receiver Justin Jefferson, two-time Pro Bowl tight end T.J. Hockenson, former first-round pick wide receiver Jordan Addison, two-time Pro Bowl quarterback Kyler Murray and an offensive line that is allowing the fifth-longest time to pressure (2.71 seconds) in the NFL this season. Yet, it has scored 12 touchdowns. That is the fewest touchdowns by a team with a 6-1 record or better through seven games since Washington in 1982.

The only team that has scored fewer touchdowns than the Vikings in 2026 is the winless Los Angeles Chargers with nine. Both the tanking Miami Dolphins (13 touchdowns) and the Deshaun Watson-led Cleveland Browns (13 touchdowns) have found the end zone more often than O'Connell's unit.

That's embarrassing, and it's grounds for a potential coaching change come the offseason if things don't improve.

The problem Minnesota has this season is that Murray isn't fitting well in O'Connell's scheme. Murray's -0.11 expected points added (EPA) per dropback is the fifth worst in the entire NFL, ahead of only Cam Ward (-0.12), Tanner McKee (-0.13), Daniel Jones (-0.19) and Justin Herbert (-0.22).

O'Connell's offense thrived with Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold heaving the ball deep down the field to Jefferson and others over the middle of the field. Murray entered 2026 ranking 40th out of 45 qualified quarterbacks in throws of 10-22 yards (intermediate throws) between the numbers (over the middle of the field). That's why his connection with Marvin Harrison Jr. failed in Arizona.

Murray much prefers throwing to the sideline with underneath completions to stay in rhythm. Just 10.7% of his throws in 2025 with the Cardinals traveled 10 or more air yards downfield, which ranked third among 42 quarterbacks with at least 150 passes last season. This season playing for O'Connell, 34.4% of Murray's throws are traveling 10 or more air yards, which is the 10th-highest rate in the NFL.

That's why he is failing in Minnesota: Murray isn't a scheme fit, but O'Connell chose him anyway. However, the Vikings head coach is publicly in denial about how things are going with his squad, which ranks as the league's sixth-worst scoring offense (20.0 points per game).

"It's going back through it. Any of the inconsistencies, really dive into the why. I don't necessarily believe it's going to be one tell-all thing," O'Connell told reporters postgame Sunday. "I think it's how we continue to put together the plans of where he's most comfortable in his alignment and then marrying the offense from there. I think we've done a good job of that."

Despite 10th overall pick J.J. McCarthy ranking dead last in the NFL in completion percentage (57.6%), touchdown-to-interception ratio (11-12) and passer rating (72.6) in his first full season as a starting quarterback in 2025, the Vikings offense was actually more efficient than it is now. Minnesota's playmakers know what the issues are. Jefferson left the locker room after the Week 8 loss without speaking to media members while Addison offered a direct assessment.

"It's not really about finding ourselves; it's just making routine plays," Addison told reporters postgame Sunday. "When you turn on the tape, we got guys open [in the pass game]. Running the ball, we got gaps that are open. We just got to execute honestly."

You know what would be an ideal situation right now? If O'Connell had the chance to sub in McCarthy for a struggling Murray to see if the former top 10 pick takes a leap after another year of season in his system. Instead, Minnesota chose to trade him away to the New York Giants in exchange for a bag of peanuts -- a 2027 fifth-round pick.

Instead, all O'Connell has is a washed-up iteration of Carson Wentz and undrafted veteran Max Brosmer, a player with no touchdown passes and four interceptions across his seven NFL games. It took O'Connell and the Vikings a few years to make enough missteps to end up in this position. One could argue the merits of letting a 36-year-old Kirk Cousins walk in free agency. But Minnesota ended up pulling a rabbit out of the hat with Darnold a year after Kyle Shanahan and the 49ers rehabbed the 2018 NFL Draft's third overall pick while making him Brock Purdy's backup.

Darnold piloted a Vikings offense that ranked No. 9 in scoring (25.4 points per game) as he threw for a career-high 35 passing touchdowns, the fifth-most in the NFL in 2024. Minnesota went 14-3 in the regular season but lost the de facto NFC North division title game in Week 18 against the Detroit Lions. Just a few weeks later, Darnold absorbed an NFL playoff-record nine sacks in a wild card round defeat against the Los Angeles Rams, souring O'Connell's perspective on his new Pro Bowl quarterback.

Instead of building upon Darnold's successful 2024 season, O'Connell decided to let the 28-year-old walk in favor of McCarthy. As mentioned earlier, McCarthy was the NFL's cellar dweller in several metrics in his first year as a starting quarterback at football's highest level at 22 years old last season. Meanwhile, in Seattle, Darnold quarterbacked the Seahawks to a Super Bowl title, throwing five touchdowns and no interceptions in his new team's three playoff games, with only six sacks. That's just an average of two sacks per game in the Seahawks' championship run.

Just like with Darnold, O'Connell decided to throw McCarthy away after one season of failure. Meanwhile in New York, McCarthy became the first Giants quarterback with at least five completions of 20-plus yards in consecutive games since Daniel Jones back in 2019. The Giants have also remained the NFC East's first-place team through eight weeks with a 4-2-1 record.

Since becoming the Vikings' head coach in 2022, O'Connell is 49-26, good for the fifth-best regular-season record in football, along with the 49ers. However, that has translated to just two postseason appearances (2022 and 2024) and no playoff wins. The two losses were the aforementioned faceplant against the Rams in the 2024 season and a 31-24 home loss against the Daniel Jones-led Giants. The next week, that same Giants team lost 38-7 at the Philadelphia Eagles in the NFC divisional round.

Two games isn't a massive sample size, but in both playoff games, O'Connell was clearly outcoached.

Four-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Justin Jefferson raced out to a historic start to his NFL career: His 7,432 yards receiving from 2020 to 2024 are the most in a player's first five seasons in league history. That production resulted in Jefferson averaging 96.5 receiving yards per game, which also ranked as the most ever in the NFL.

Then, J.J. McCarthy happened. McCarthy wasn't ready for the speed of the NFL game, ranking dead last in the entire league in completion percentage (57.6%), touchdown-to-interception ratio (11-12), and passer rating (72.6) in 2025. His ineptitude led to Jefferson posting career lows in receiving yards (1,048) and receiving touchdowns (2) in 2025, which dropped his receiving yards per game average down to 90.2 -- the second-most in NFL history behind Puka Nacua's 95.3 average.

Now, Kyler Murray is a poor scheme fit, which has Jefferson averaging a career-low 55.8 receiving yards per game in 2026. That's brought his career average down to 88.2 receiving yards per game. Jefferson still has a pathway toward being an all-timer -- he still has 8,815 career receiving yards through his first 100 games -- but he can see that path narrowing under O'Connell the last two seasons. That's why he let loose a rare display of public frustration on the sideline on Sunday.

Justin Jefferson Is Clearly Pissed On The Sideline.Overthrown, Underthrown, And Watching Kyler Miss Him All Day.And The Trade Deadline Is This Week.Just Saying. 👀📞 https://t.co/slF8rftvzX pic.twitter.com/VPueiaCCVl

O'Connell's and Murray's lack of offensive synergy wasn't fully exposed until the 19-15 loss at the Lions on Sunday. Five of their six wins to begin the year were against teams that are outside the playoff picture or had a starting quarterback injury in the middle of the game.

The Vikings beat the Packers, a current playoff team with a 5-3 record, 39-22 in Week 1 before beating the Chicago Bears 9-3 in Week 2 after Bears quarterback Caleb Williams departed with a hamstring injury. The other four wins were against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (23-16), the Miami Dolphins (15-10), the New Orleans Saints (23-13) and the Indianapolis Colts (16-10). The best record of those squads, outside of Green Bay and Chicago, belongs to the 3-5 Buccaneers.

Now, the Vikings' offensive issues stand to be majorly exposed over the next three weeks. Minnesota plays the Bills (6-1) on "Monday Night Football" in Week 9, at Lambeau Field against the Packers in Week 10 and at the 49ers on "Sunday Night Football" in Week 11. That's the toughest stretch of games in the NFL from Weeks 8-11.

Some team could soon be banging down Flores' door after the defensive masterclass he is putting together this season. That puts the Vikings in a spot where they may have to lose one of the best defensive masterminds in football next offseason. If Minnesota ends up missing the playoffs or fails to win a playoff game, wasting what is shaping up to be an all-time year from its defense, O'Connell would certainly face -- and earn -- heightened scrutiny.

Perhaps there's a chance O'Connell's job could go to Flores by promoting him to be their head coach instead of losing him to another team. Regardless, O'Connell's lack of success in evaluating his quarterback position, despite his reputation as a "quarterback guru," along with wasting Justin Jefferson and a lack of results in the playoffs, deserves plenty of skepticism, 6-1 record be damned.

#2689. 2026 MLB Gold Glove winners: Pete Crow-Armstrong wins second honor, Red Sox and D-backs lead with three each

The winners of the 2026 Rawlings Gold Glove were announced Sunday night by Major League Baseball and, as expected, Cubs wunderkind Pete Crow-Armstrong took home his second straight National League Gold Glove in center field. PCA, who also won a Gold Glove in 2025 and is expected to be named the NL MVP in 2026, was the best defender in baseball this past season based on both the numbers and the eye test.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Crow-Armstrong's +26 FRV is the fifth best in a single season since FRV launched in 2016 and the second best by a non-catcher, trailing only Nick Ahmed's +28 FRV season at shortstop in 2018.

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. Now the outfield spots are broken down into left field, center field, and right field.

Winners are determined through manager/coach voting (75%) and a statistical component (25%). Team employees can not vote for their own players.

While MLB announced "finalists" for each Gold Glove a few weeks back, remember that the voting was already complete and those finalists were simply the top three vote-getters at each position. This means, obviously, that postseason performance had no impact. Here now are the 2026 Gold Glove winners.

Brandon Valenzuela (Blue Jays) and Austin Wells (Yankees)

Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (Blue Jays) and Vinnie Pasquantino (Royals)

Freddy Fermin (Padres) and Luis Torrens (Mets)

Ty France (Padres) and TJ Rumfield (Rockies)

Brandon Lowe (Pirates) and JJ Wetherholt (Cardinals)

Dansby Swanson (Cubs) and Masyn Winn (Cardinals)

Max Muncy (Dodgers) and Javier Sanoja (Marlins)

Ian Happ (Cubs) and Daylen Lile (Nationals)

Michael Harris II (Braves) and Andy Pages (Dodgers)

Carson Benge (Mets) and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs)

Michael McGreevy (Cardinals) and Chris Sale (Braves)

Jared Triolo (Pirates) and Ildemaro Vargas (Diamondbacks)

#2687. 2026 midseason rookie grades: Ranking the early hits, misses and biggest surprises

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight weeks into the NFL season, we're starting to get some answers about the 2026 first-round rookie class. Some players look exactly like we thought they would when they came out of college. Others have been pleasant surprises. And then there are those still struggling with some of the same issues that showed up on their college tape.

We evaluated these rookies after four weeks on the With the First Pick podcast – it was our most popular episode this fall – and Arvell Reese and Sonny Styles were among the early standouts. David Bailey was still finding his footing, Rueben Bain Jr. was battling injuries, and Dillon Thieneman looked like one of the league's most promising young safeties.

A month later, some of those evaluations look a little (and, in some cases, a lot) different.

These are our first-half grades for all 32 first-round picks from the 2026 class, based on everything we've seen through eight weeks. Production matters, but so do injuries, expectations and what the tape reveals. We're also revisiting our original scouting reports from the 2026 draft cycle to see which traits have translated, which concerns have followed these players to the NFL, and where we might have missed something. And because good players aren't limited to the first round, we've also graded 10 rookies drafted on Days 2 and 3 who have already made their mark.

Mendoza finally got on the field in Week 5 mop-up duty vs. the Patriots. He was a tidy 6 of 8 for 48 yards. For now, veteran Kirk Cousins remains the starter, but as the losses pile up, Mendoza will likely get his chance to be QB1.

Bailey has taken a noticeable step forward after an uneven start, highlighted by a three-sack performance against Cleveland. I loved his explosive first step, speed-to-power, inside spin and relentless motor at Texas Tech, and we're seeing all of it in the NFL. What's been particularly encouraging is his development against the run, where Jets coaches have praised his discipline and ability to handle responsibilities beyond rushing the passer. He's becoming the complete defender New York envisioned when it drafted him second overall.

Love hasn't looked like the explosive, home-run threat we watched at Notre Dame, but there's a very simple reason: He's been battling an ankle injury since the preseason, and it cost him two games. At Notre Dame, I loved his ability to accelerate through the smallest crease and turn ordinary runs into big plays, but Love has acknowledged that he hasn't been able to cut or explode the way he did in college (not yet, anyway). This grade really doesn't mean much until we see what a healthy version of Love looks like. And that won't be for at least another month with today's trip to the IR.

Tate is becoming a dependable target for Cam Ward despite Tennessee's offensive struggles, and that's hardly surprising given how polished he looked at Ohio State. His ability to manipulate DBs, separate at the top of routes and make difficult catches look easy gave him a chance to contribute immediately. Tate continues to get more comfortable in Tennessee's offense, and he's showing the makings of a No. 1 receiver.

Remember all those concerns about Reese's pro day workout? Seven months later and he's one of the easiest evaluations in the class because he's doing exactly what made him such an exciting prospect at Ohio State. Instincts, range, and insane athleticism, while learning on the job, have all made him an immediate difference-maker, and Giants coaches have praised how quickly he's hit the ground running.

Delane looked like a grizzled All-Pro from the moment he stepped on the field. The only issue has been staying healthy. He was one of the most technically sound CBs in the draft and that has immediately translated – even when he's "allowed" receptions while in coverage (show me the human who is stopping JSN – also, look at Delane's coverage!). The Chiefs traded up for Delane and so far, it appears that they nailed this pick.

Washington already trusts Styles to relay defensive calls and make adjustments before the snap, impressive responsibilities for a rookie still relatively new to playing off-ball LB. His instincts and athleticism stood out at Ohio State, and he's carried those strengths into the NFL. He's been particularly effective in coverage vs. TEs and RBs, and he's shown consistent improvement against the run. There have been occasional missed tackles, but through eight weeks, he's been one of the best players in this rookie class.

The issue with Tyson in college was staying healthy. Those issues remain.

Cleveland appears to have found its long-term answer at left tackle. Fano's footwork, balance and ability to recover against high-end edge rushers were some of the reasons I liked him so much coming out of Utah. And even though he's moved from right to left tackle for the Browns, he's doing a lot of the same things really well.

The move from college tackle to NFL guard hasn't been seamless, but Mauigoa has steadily gotten better. His athleticism and ability to move defenders in the running game stood out at Miami, although he occasionally struggled with balance and hand placement. Those issues have followed him inside, but his improved pass protection, especially vs. Houston in Week 7, was encouraging.

Few prospects were easier to trust coming out of college than Downs, whose instincts, anticipation and IQ made him special at Ohio State. This is what makes his recent NFL struggles so surprising (I gave him a B+ through the first month of the season). Opponents have completed 20 of 24 passes against him for 230 yards and three touchdowns, and poor pursuit angles have contributed to explosive runs. Dallas expected a defensive centerpiece, not a liability in coverage, as CBS Sports' Garrett Podell detailed.

Proctor has been candid about his struggles moving inside, acknowledging that speed of the game in confined spaces -- something he didn't have to deal with at Alabama -- creates bigger problems at guard. His rare athleticism remains obvious, but the balance and hand-placement concerns from his college tape haven't disappeared. A Week 7 concussion hasn't helped, keeping him sidelined for Week 8's loss to the Patriots.

Remember when we all gawked and pointed at the Rams' arrogance for taking Simpson when there were bigger, more immediate needs? I suppose that case can still be made … but it also doesn't look like Matthew Stafford has another year or two left in him.

Baltimore has already needed Ioane to play center because of injuries, and he's handled the transition well. His powerful hands, leverage and ability to anchor made him one of my favorite interior linemen at Penn State. He's brought that same reliability to Baltimore, although an MCL injury has interrupted an otherwise encouraging start. And while our old buddy Rick Spielman wasn't a fan of plus/minus when grading players, I'm giving Ioane an extra plus for his versatility.

It's taken a bit, but we're finally seeing the player who was a game wrecker at Miami. Shoulder and groin injuries derailed Bain's first month, but his explosive first step, violent hands and ability to generate power are showing up more consistently as he gets healthy. The production hasn't matched expectations yet, although he's trending in the right direction.

Remember Sadiq's seven-catch, 105-yard performance against Detroit? That's the explosive mismatch weapon we saw at Oregon. But his opportunities have diminished with Mason Taylor back in the lineup, and a Week 5 concussion only complicated matters. The encouraging part? His blocking has been better than expected, even if the receiving production hasn't followed.

Miller's pass protection has been one of the more encouraging developments among all rookie offensive linemen. His balance, lateral agility and ability to redirect stood out at Clemson, and he's handled NFL edge rushers surprisingly well over the first two months. The running game is another story; he hasn't been nearly as good play in and play out.

Minnesota knew Banks was a developmental prospect, but he's played just 25% of the defensive snaps and hasn't made much of an impact. When healthy, his twitch, lateral quickness and ability to penetrate made him a lot of fun to watch at Florida. The problem? Once blockers get their hands on him, particularly on double teams, he struggles to disengage. Those concerns haven't disappeared, and his limited playing time suggests the Vikings aren't ready to trust him with a bigger role. I'm giving Banks an incomplete here, in part because we knew this would be a process, in part because Dallas Turner needed a couple of years in Brian Flores' system before figuring it out.

Freeling deserves credit for responding well when Carolina needed him earlier than expected, and at a position (RT) he didn't play in college. A knee injury hasn't helped his development, and right now, he's more of a developmental prospect than a reliable starter.

After a quiet September that left a lot of folks wondering if Sean Mannion knew Lemon was on the roster, the USC standout is finally starting to look like the first-round talent we saw last fall for the Trojans. His toughness, reliable hands and ability to create after the catch have become more evident as his role expands. There have been some drops, but he's one of the few bright spots in an otherwise forgettable season in Philly.

Iheanachor hasn't avoided rookie mistakes, but what's encouraging is how he's responded to them. His quick feet, power and lateral movement skills were obvious at Arizona State, even if he was incredibly raw. He's still raw, but he's shown an ability to quickly make adjustments instead of repeating the same mistakes.

Despite all that's gone wrong with the Chargers, Mesidor has been one of the bright spots, and his coaches have explained why: he's stopped overthinking and started trusting his instincts. The heavy hands, leverage, versatility and non-stop motor that made him a first-rounder out of Miami are showing up more consistently. He's playing faster, even if the production doesn't always reflect it.

Lawrence's first NFL sack offered a glimpse of the explosiveness that made him stand out at UCF. His first-step quickness and power were impressive in college, but limited bend meant he'd need to develop better counters and hand usage. That's all still a work in progress, and the reality is that Dallas hasn't gotten consistent production from him. In his defense, they've gotten consistent production from exactly no one on this defense.

Concepcion has been better than advertised and the advertisements were pretty good coming out of Texas A&M. His suddenness and precise route running have immediately translated. Browns coaches have also praised his preparation and ability to learn multiple receiver positions, giving Cleveland more ways to get him involved. GM Andrew Berry has quietly crushed another draft class.

A month ago, Thieneman looked like one of the pleasant surprises of Round 1 (I gave him a B+ at the quarter pole). His instincts, range and willingness to attack downhill were everything we saw at Oregon. But the concerns about flipping his hips and tracking receivers downfield have resurfaced, and now opponents are increasingly testing him vertically. His second month hasn't been nearly as impressive as his first, but there's still a ton to be excited about.

Houston drafted Rutledge to add some much-needed nastiness up front, but his pass protection has been a problem. To be fair, the Texans have asked him to learn all three interior o-line positions after playing almost exclusively right guard at Georgia Tech. Still, poor balance, hand placement and recognition have made him vulnerable, and the physical tools remain more impressive than the results. Overall, I'm going to grade him on a curve because he's been asked to do a lot in a short span.

Johnson is becoming more dependable as Miami moves him between outside corner and the slot. His competitiveness, recovery speed and ability to stay in phase on shorter routes were strengths at San Diego State, and we're seeing that now show up on Sundays. Bottom line: He's made real progress since September, when I gave him a C.

Lomu has played only about 160 snaps -- far fewer than most of the first-round rookie offensive linemen -- but he's made the most of his opportunities. He was impressive against the Jets in Week 6. Filling in for an injured Morgan Moses, he played 60 snaps at right tackle, allowed zero pressures and held his own against David Bailey. His quick feet and balance were strengths at Utah, and they're serving him well as he adjusts to the NFL. I gave him an incomplete here but if pressed, I'd give him a B-.

Woods was one of the most physically gifted defenders in this class, which makes his uneven start a little frustrating. His explosiveness, leverage and ability to disrupt running plays have translated from Clemson, but he hasn't been nearly as effective rushing the passer. He still struggles with double teams, and his inability to consistently win one-on-one as a pass rusher remains a concern.

Two consecutive 100-yard games after returning from injured reserve? That'll work. Cooper's toughness, contested-catch ability and knack for making difficult receptions look routine were how he made his name at Indiana. He's already developing chemistry with Geno Smith, and while it's a small sample, there's a lot to like.

Faulk's length and power made him an appealing first-round prospect at Auburn, but he hasn't consistently turned those tools into on-field production. An early sack against the Giants offered a glimpse of his potential. Since then, he's struggled when OTs have neutralized his initial pass-rush move. He'll need to diversify his pass-rush arsenal, something that showed up on tape in college but was less of an issue because he was routinely the freakiest athlete on the field.

Price's chest injury has left us with little to evaluate. He got off to a promising start in Week 1, rushing for 52 yards on 10 carries, but played just two more games before landing on injured reserve. He also lost fumbles in both of those appearances. The talent we saw at Notre Dame is still there, but we've barely seen it in Seattle.

Of course, the first round isn't the only place teams find impact players. Here are some Day 2 names who have stood out through the first half of their rookie seasons -- and in some cases, are already outperforming players drafted well ahead of them.

Boston has given Cleveland a legitimate downfield threat, with 409 receiving yards and three touchdowns through eight games. His size, body control and ability to win contested catches have translated from Washington, although defenses have done a better job limiting his explosive plays recently.

Rodriguez has wasted little time becoming an important part of Miami's defense, relying on the instincts, play recognition and tackling ability that made him so productive at Texas Tech. He may not have elite athletic traits, but he consistently finds the football and has been one of the more impressive second-round rookies.

Jacas has been a problem for opposing offensive tackles, generating 21 pressures through his first seven games. His power, bend and ability to diagnose plays have stood out on film, and he's already producing like a player who should have been drafted higher.

McNeil-Warren has earned an expanding role in Cleveland's secondary, where his length, physicality, closing speed and versatility have helped the Browns disguise coverages. The instincts and willingness to attack downhill that stood out at Toledo are serving him well, and he's developing into a valuable piece of the defense.

Bernard has taken advantage of Pittsburgh's injuries at receiver, becoming an increasingly reliable target for Aaron Rodgers. His route awareness, toughness, blocking and ability to line up in multiple spots have translated from Alabama, while his preparation and willingness to learn have earned praise from the coaching staff.

And then there are the Day 3 picks, where finding immediate contributors becomes a little more difficult -- and sometimes the evaluations look a lot different with the benefit of hindsight. For these five rookies, I've included my original pre-draft grade, final big board ranking and what I liked about them coming out of college, if only to see what I got right, what I missed and whether these teams saw something I didn't.

My pre-draft grade: 3rd–4th round | Final big board rank: No. 98

Why I liked him: An explosive, one-gap penetrator with surprising power, active hands and a relentless motor who could disrupt plays before offensive linemen established their blocks.

Halton has been one of the biggest Day 3 steals, making an immediate impact on San Francisco's defensive line with 15 tackles, two sacks and a forced fumble through six games. His first-step quickness, ability to disengage from blockers and relentless motor have all helped him become an integral part of the rotation.

My pre-draft grade: 3rd round | Final big board rank: No. 84

Why I liked him: A physical, aggressive slot defender who could cover, blitz off the edge and blow up running plays near the line of scrimmage.

Scott might be the best example of a Day 3 rookie playing well beyond his draft position (though he slipped on draft day because of off-field concerns). He's already established himself as Tampa Bay's starting nickel, where his physicality, quick trigger and versatility have made him a valuable part of Todd Bowles' defense. Bowles has praised his toughness and tackling.

My pre-draft grade: 4th round | Final big board rank: No. 122

Why I liked him: A powerful, high-motor edge defender with heavy hands, a strong lower half and the ability to set the edge against the run.

Dennis-Sutton has given Green Bay valuable pass-rush production, generating 15 pressures through seven weeks and earning more playing time as a result. His power, heavy hands and ability to hold up against the run were obvious at Penn State, but he's also shown more as a pass rusher than I expected.

My pre-draft grade: 7th–UDFA | Final big board rank: No. 300

Why I liked him: A physical, downhill linebacker with length, straight-line speed and the willingness to take on blockers, although his lateral stiffness and coverage limitations were significant concerns.

Dugger has become a valuable part of San Francisco's defense, playing more than half the defensive snaps and recording 30 tackles through seven games. A former safety still learning the nuances of off-ball LB, he's making excellent use of his range, closing speed and versatility, with the coaching staff trusting him in coverage and as a blitzer. Also goes to show that sometimes one person's evaluation can miss the mark (and sometimes by a good bit).

My pre-draft grade: 4th round | Final big board rank: No. 134

Why I liked him: A versatile hybrid defender with outstanding range, physicality and some of the best open-field tackling ability in the class, capable of making plays from the slot, box or edge.

One of my 2026 draft sleepers, Daniels has been one of the most impressive Day 3 picks of the class, starting all eight games with 53 tackles, four tackles for loss, a sack and an interception. His range, versatility and ability to finish tackles in space were among the reasons I thought he might sneak into Day 2, and he's already becoming an important part of Jeff Ulbrich's defense.

#2686. Inter Milan U19: Team Analysis – MH

von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

Inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place. They also secured victory in the knockout playoff round and will now face Bayern Munich U19 in the Round of 16. This analysis will take a closer look at Inter Milan’s tactical structures and mechanisms under head coach Andrea Zanchetta in the Youth League while also considering possible approaches against them.

Inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape. A key role is played by the midfield trio, consisting of the two number eights, Topalovic and Venturini, alongside the single pivot, Mattia Zanchetta. Zanchetta frequently drops between the center-backs, taking on a key role in deep buildup, while the two eights serve as connectors and overload players in the transition from deeper buildup into more advanced areas. According to the Italian Wikipedia, head coach Andrea Zanchetta is the father of Mattia Zanchetta.

Inter’s defensive structure varies depending on the opponent and pressing height. In mid-block and high-pressing phases, they defend in a narrow 4-3-2-1, a compact 4-3-3, or a 4-4-2, depending on the opposition’s structure. When defending deeper, they shift into a 4-1-4-1, with Zanchetta holding his position as the single pivot shielding the backline.

As the central striker, either Lavelli or Spinaccè leads the line. Since both share a similar physical, robust playing style, this analysis will primarily refer to Spinaccè, who has started in recent matches. On the right wing, Pieri is a fixed starter, known for his strong 1v1 abilities. On the opposite flank, head coach Zanchetta has rotated more frequently, but he has consistently relied on technically strong, dribble-oriented wingers.

To build up against high pressing, Inter relies on certain patterns that make it more difficult for the opponent to press successfully. A frequent observation is that the center-backs move wide while the full-backs push up along the touchline. At the same time, the single pivot Zanchetta and/or the number eight Topalovic drop deep to lure the opposition’s midfield out of the center. The longer the possession phase lasts near their own penalty area, the more likely it is that both the pivot and the number eight drop into the center-back positions. The now-vacated central space is occupied by the other number eight, Venturini, and the frequently dropping center-forward Spinaccè. When buildup occurs on the right side, Topalovic often stays on the far side to stretch the central area further. The wingers act as additional passing options by tucking into the half-spaces. From this structure, the opponent can be bypassed using vertical-layoff combinations in the half-space.

The primary goal of the buildup is often a pass to the target man Spinaccè, who either uses Venturini as a layoff option or directly switches play to the wing. By pulling apart the central space through the movements of Topalovic and Zanchetta, the goalkeeper typically initiates buildup through the wide center-backs, who frequently play a direct pass to the dropping striker via the now-open diagonal deep passing lane. Particularly noteworthy are the anticipatory movements of the layoff options in these combinations. The attacking number eight, Venturini, excels at positioning himself to receive layoffs from the back-to-goal striker Spinaccè, ensuring continuity in progression.

If only Zanchetta drops between the center-backs to form the resulting back three, the left-sided number eight, Topalovic, and the right-sided number eight, Venturini, move into the half-spaces to receive when the center-backs are in possession. Through a vertical-layoff combination involving one of the eights, the now-advancing pivot Zanchetta, and the dropping center-forward Spinaccè, the midfield can be quickly bypassed, allowing the ball to be switched to the wing in the opponent’s half.

To effectively press Inter’s buildup directly, a hybrid pressing approach combining man- and space-orientation could be a viable strategy. A particularly crucial role could be assigned to the ball-far holding midfielder, who could operate positionally to close passing lanes, preventing deep balls into the target man Spinaccè while also ensuring that the central space cannot be stretched. Additionally, an aggressive step-out from a center-back would be necessary to avoid numerical inferiority in midfield. On the ball-near side, increased pressure could be applied through man-oriented marking to maximize pressing intensity.

Through hybrid pressing, the center can be occupied, and the typical passing lane can be blocked. The downside is the numerical disadvantage on the ball-far side and the man-to-man marking on the last line.

Even against teams that press deeper, certain patterns can be observed in Inter Milan U19’s buildup. From their usual 4-3-3 structure with a single pivot and two number eights, they transition into a three-man buildup shape against opponents using a two-striker system. To achieve this, Zanchetta drops between the center-backs, who move wider, while the full-backs push higher along the touchline. However, Zanchetta plays a flexible role, shifting between a central center-back position and his original pivot role, making himself available in midfield depending on the situation.

This three-man buildup creates new passing connections designed to pose problems for the opponent. A key role is played by Topalovic and Venturini, who drop closer to the buildup to fill the emerging gap between the midfield and the first buildup line. The buildup is primarily conducted through the half-spaces and the wide areas. The ball-near number eight moves into the half-space to overload it, while Venturini, from the right half-space, moves into an advanced position, and Topalovic, from the left half-space, stays closer to the buildup zone, occasionally even dropping into the first line. The ball-far number eight occupies the center.

Due to this asymmetry between the two eights, the wingers on each side have slightly different roles. On the right side, where Venturini often occupies the advanced half-space, the right winger stays wider, creating double width with the full-back. On the left side, since Topalovic supports deeper in the buildup, the left winger frequently moves into the half-space, opening the lane for the overlapping full-back on the outside.

Additionally, Spinaccè overloads the half-space by shifting ball-near and dropping deeper. Particularly on the left side, a diagonal deep pass from the wide-positioned center-back in the back three can find either the winger or the striker in a diagonal alignment. This escadinha staggering provides multiple layoff options. The ultimate goal after playing through the half-space is to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, allowing the dribbling-strong wingers or advancing full-backs to be isolated and attack down the flank.

Through the typical half-space overload, the wide area can be opened for a 1v1 situation involving the advancing full-back.

The follow-up action is usually a cross into the penalty area. This is typically occupied by the aerially strong striker, the ball-far winger, and Topalovic. In the second line, Zanchetta and Venturini can win second balls.

One of the key aspects of Inter Milan’s game is their man-marking high press. With the exception of the match against Manchester City, coach Zanchetta’s team has consistently relied on man-marking and aggressive pressing in advanced areas. This approach frequently creates dangerous transition moments by forcing early turnovers.

While striker Spinaccè and the right winger are primarily responsible for initiating the press, Topalovic and Zanchetta operate in central areas. Zanchetta, known for his strength in duels, pushes far forward from his usual deeper pivot position to press opposing midfielders and win the ball in central areas. The offensively oriented number eight, Venturini, is deliberately kept out of direct 1v1 defensive duels in the center and instead takes responsibility for a potentially advancing full-back. On the opposite side, the opposing full-back is covered by Inter’s winger.

The pressing is almost always triggered by Spinaccè from a slightly left-sided position. He presses the goalkeeper while blocking the passing lane to the left center-back. This forces the opponent’s buildup toward the wing, where Inter engages in their man-oriented pressing. In particular, the ball-far midfielder, Topalovic, often abandons his direct man-marking after the opponent is forced to play toward the far-side wing. Instead, he drops back toward the defensive line to create numerical superiority and ensure that the center-backs can step out aggressively without leaving gaps in the last line.

A possible solution against this man-marking press could involve putting the opposing center-backs in a dilemma. By having the strikers drop deep, they could force the center-backs to abandon their cover in the last line. Since Inter Milan’s full-backs are less dominant in defensive 1v1 situations, wingers making deep diagonal runs into the vacated spaces could create a favorable scenario. Once the press is triggered, these wingers should be played into 1v1 situations through deep passes. This either forces the physically strong center-backs out of the last line or creates a numerical superiority in midfield that can be exploited.

Another possible approach could involve a high-positioned, inverted left-back. By dropping into the space between the opponent’s forward and midfield lines, he could create a central 1v1 against Venturini, who is not as defensively strong.

Depending on the opponent, Inter may drop slightly deeper and defend in a 4-3-3 or 4-4-2 mid-block shape. This adjustment depends on the opposition’s buildup structure. The fundamental goal is to maintain numerical parity against the opponent’s buildup line, allowing Inter to transition into aggressive man-marking and press forward. Against a three-man buildup, they press in a 4-3-3 shape, while against a four-man buildup, they shift into a 4-4-2. A key emphasis is placed on central compactness, making it more difficult for the opponent to progress through the middle.

Once the ball is shifted to one side, Inter looks to apply pressure and enforce man-marking, similar to their approach in the high press. Zanchetta frequently pushes forward aggressively on the ball-near side to put pressure on the opponent’s central midfielders and create ball-winning opportunities.

While the full-backs also push high to apply pressure, the center-backs primarily serve as defensive cover. However, when the opposition’s strikers drop deeper, the center-backs do not follow them to avoid leaving gaps in the defensive line. Instead, Inter presses with one less player in the first line to compensate for the opponent’s numerical superiority in midfield. Even in these situations, the opponent is guided toward one side, where Inter then looks to regain possession. To execute this, the first pressing line must initially cut off the passing lane to one of the defenders, allowing the opponent to maintain more possession and reducing Inter’s ability to transition into their man-marking press.

Especially in the low block, Inter Milan manages to make the field so compact that progression becomes extremely difficult. From a 4-1-4-1 structure, they compress the space just in front of their own penalty area. Zanchetta operates between the lines as a space-oriented pivot in front of the defense. When the opponent shifts play to one side, Zanchetta also moves laterally and looks to engage an opposing player.

As the central players shift heavily toward the ball side, defensive numerical superiority is often created near the ball, allowing Inter to apply pressure. The ball-far number eight secures the central area, while the ball-far winger stays wide when the opponent maintains width on both flanks to prevent switches of play. This enables the last defensive line to shift further toward the ball side, allowing the ball-near center-back to step out aggressively while still being covered.

Inter Milan’s U19 team manages to challenge opponents through a well-organized and versatile defensive structure. They can adapt to various pressing heights, with their difficult-to-play man-marking high press frequently creating dangerous transition moments close to the opponent’s goal.

In possession, Inter also succeeds in reaching the opponent’s penalty area frequently through a very direct approach aimed at attacking depth. The key to this is a well-coordinated midfield and a striker who can act as a target player, holding up the ball with his back to goal. Most of Inter’s combinations are designed to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, where both the advancing full-backs and the wingers are very difficult to defend.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2685. MLB Power Rankings: Brewers end 2026 season at No. 1 as World Series champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I'm done. No more. Enough is enough. I have doubted the Brewers far too many times and I decided in early August to never do it again. I started picking them to win the World Series every chance I got. I was finally right.

Every time they traded away someone good (the latest being Freddy Peralta last offseason), I thought, "OK, now is when it finally catches up with them." Only it never does. I thought they needed Tarik Skubal, both to reinforce their rotation and also to keep him away from the Dodgers. It didn't matter. They beat him and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS.

It's a juggernaut of an organization. They churn out talent and get the most out of every player they have. They seem to trade away talent at the exact right time. They develop young stars better than anyone. There's another one coming in Jesús Made, but there's no reason for Brewers fans to dream about the future when the present is World Series champions.

Jackson Chourio is becoming a superstar, Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young and Christian Yelich is a former MVP, but it isn't really about the big names with this group. It's everything. It's the entire team making this train run, working as a cohesive unit. It's Robert Gasser going out and dealing in Game 3 after starting the season in the minors. It's Jake Bauers winning NLCS MVP not too long after he was ready to retire from baseball. It's Aaron Ashby putting up one of the greatest reliever performances in playoff history. It's Sal Frelick hitting a game-tying bomb. It's Cooper Pratt's coming-out party in the World Series. And on and on and on we could go.

Milwaukee is the best organization in baseball now, supplanting the former two-time defending champion Dodgers.

The Brewers head to next season with plenty of question marks, but they'll answer them. They always do. They are the champions of Major League Baseball and they sit atop the final 2026 Power Rankings.

Looking forward to next spring, my expectation is the Brewers will be No. 1. Some years, I write about why the defending champion is not No. 1. I've long since learned my lesson with this team, though. No more. The Brewers will be No. 1 heading into spring training.

#2684. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Last unbeaten team is ... the Grizzlies? Plus a crisis in OKC

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We couldn't even settle in before the season went sideways, could we? After a relatively ordinary first few days, the entire NBA seemed to catch the injury bug in Week 2. A seemingly endless list of All-Stars went down in the past seven days with injuries that will keep them out for periods ranging from a few weeks to, potentially, the entire season, and after just 13 days of basketball, the league-wide landscape suddenly looks completely different.

So let's look back on the week that was and rank some winners and losers from the NBA's last seven days.

Raise a glass for the NBA's last unbeaten team, the... Memphis Grizzlies? Huh? Yes, the Memphis Grizzlies, one of last season's most egregious tankers, are running roughshod over the rest of the NBA. As of Sunday afternoon, they rank...

Even after cooling off following his preposterously hot start, Ty Jerome has still made more runners (19) than all but a handful of players have attempted. Jerome may be cooling off, but Cam Boozer is heating up: the No. 3 overall pick just shot 50-44-100 for the week and picked up his first career triple-double in a win over the then-unbeaten Portland Trail Blazers (and former Grizzlies star Ja Morant). Nobody can miss a 3. Zech Edey and Isaiah Stewart are almost completely walling off the rim. Grizzlies opponents are taking only 19 shots per game in the restricted area.

The pick-and-roll-heavy scheme Tuomas Iisalo was known for abroad is finally coming together in the NBA. Only the Cleveland Cavaliers have generated more shots out of pick-and-roll than Memphis. Only the Miami Heat and Houston Rockets are scoring more points per possession on those shots. After Iisalo's short-stint rotations caused so much of an uproar last season, Memphis has gotten off to this start with nobody averaging even 32 minutes a game.

Memphis won't be this good forever. They've played a Charmin soft schedule. Eventually, they'll start missing 3s, and Jerome will probably settle somewhere between the MVP frontrunner he was in Week 1 and the far less effective player we saw in Week 2. But all of this winning isn't a fluke. It's not as though their opponents are just missing shots. They're killing the teams that they're playing. Even if 82-0 is unrealistic, a playoff berth certainly feels realistic for a Grizzlies team that is thriving to start the season.

Nobody roots for injuries, but teams certainly benefit from them. We came into the season assuming the Thunder and Spurs were heavy championship favorites. The Thunder are suddenly in peril, and the Rockets beat San Antonio head-to-head in the season's opening week. They have one of the few big men in the NBA in Alperen Sengun who seems genuinely comfortable attacking Victor Wembanyama. He shot 17 of 23 against Wembanyama as the primary defender last season, according to NBA.com tracking data. He just dropped a 29-7-7 on him in Houston's second game of the year. The stars are aligning for the Rockets already.

This isn't purely a matter of circumstance, either. Houston has clearly leveled up with Fred VanVleet back in the fold. They'd likely be standing alongside the Grizzlies in the ranks of the undefeated had Sengun not missed Friday's loss to the Dallas Mavericks. After a year of consternation about their mess of a half-court offense, Houston ranks fourth in the NBA in points per 100 half-court plays thus far this season. They have the NBA's No. 1 overall offense despite barely getting any minutes out Steven Adams so far. Just imagine how easily they'll score with his offensive rebounding in the mix.

The season is far too young to say anything definitively, especially with injuries coming so quickly. For now, at least, Houston should feel relatively safe about outwinning Oklahoma City in the regular season, and it has a one-game lead and a head-to-head victory over San Antonio in its back pocket. The No. 1 seed feels much more attainable to them than it did two weeks ago, and with it would come the easiest possible path to the NBA Finals.

The consensus surrounding Lendeborg as a draft prospect was that, as a 24-year-old on opening night, he would arrive in the NBA as a productive player, but would have limited upside to grow beyond that. He's older than Jonathan Kuminga, after all, so it's not as though his arrival heralded the emergence of yet another timeline. At this rate, though, it might not matter if Lendeborg has already peaked as an NBA player, because the last week suggests he might have arrived in the NBA as a star.

His collegiate career-high in scoring was 30 points. He's topped that figure twice in the last week alone, and it's not as though he's doing that with crazy volume. His season-high in shot attempts (20) is Darius Acuff's season-low. His only bad game of the week came in his hyped rematch with Luka Dončić... a game the Golden State Warriors still managed to win despite Lendeborg claiming he "wet the bed."

Lendeborg's emergence has a chance to be genuinely transformative for Golden State. Suddenly the Warriors have the secondary scorer they need next to Curry. When Jimmy Butler returns, they'll have one of the most physically imposing pairs of forwards in the NBA, helping to offset their size issues at center with Kristaps Porziņģis sidelined. Maybe Lendeborg is even good enough to compel Golden State to attach draft picks to Porziņģis' contract and go make a win-now move. A week ago, the Warriors were winless and limping their way through a hopeless season. They've since won four straight and generated their first real dose of optimism since Butler tore his ACL, and it's almost entirely because of a rookie that somehow slipped out of the top 10 of the draft.

On Monday, the Thunder announced that both Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace would have surgeries that could end their seasons. That night, they lost Alex Caruso to a sprained ankle. That's a year's worth of injury news in a night, and then on Friday, it came out Chet Holmgren has a small patellar tendon tear that will require an 8-10 week absence following a "biological" treatment. What exactly that means for his long-term health prospects is unclear.

The Thunder opened the season by avenging their Western Conference Finals loss to the San Antonio Spurs. They followed that up by dispatching the player team that pushed them to the brink in the 2025 playoffs: Nikola Jokić and the Denver Nuggets. They looked like heavy championship favorites.

Now? It's possible that they reached the point of no return on injuries before Halloween, and if they haven't now, they could at any moment. We went from "the Thunder are the best team in the NBA" to "the Thunder could trade their way back into the championship picture" to "does it really make sense for the Thunder to start their luxury tax in this nightmare season?" all in the span of a few days. That last question is still months away from an answer, but the fact that it's even on the table is a testament to just how disastrous the last week or so has been in Oklahoma City.

We have our first reports of an unhappy team in this early season, and it is one of last year's surprise success stories: the Phoenix Suns. On Thursday, Chris Haynes explained that "there is some growing frustration within that locker room for the simple fact that that roster does not have a point guard that can organize that offense."

We should clarify here that the Suns do have a point guard on their roster... they're just not starting him. The Suns are scoring 123.2 points per 100 possessions with Collin Gillespie on the floor... and 106.4 with him off it, according to Cleaning the Glass. Pretty much all of the underlying numbers suggest that simply starting Gillespie over Jalen Green could solve some of these point guard issues. The Suns assist on 76.3% of their baskets with Gillespie on the floor so far this season, but only 54.2% of them with him off it. Devin Booker has a 68.1% true shooting percentage with Gillespie playing and a 51.3% mark without him.

The decision to start Green was a questionable one even before the season started. He wasn't really a part of last season's success. He was a No. 2 overall pick, sure, but that was for a different team. The Suns don't have enough invested in Green to justify the continued usage of these suboptimal lineups. They frankly have too many real problems to continue creating more of them for themselves with suboptimal lineup decisions.

The Suns had a top-10 defense a year ago. They rank 30th early in this season. Their dominant offensive rebounding has slipped to the middle of the pack as well, and even their turnover rate has ticked up a bit. The Suns beat expectations last season because they were disciplined and they played harder than anyone in the league. They've fallen from No. 5 to No. 26 in deflections per game this season, and No. 6 to No. 26 in loose ball recoveries. These aren't the hustle Suns of a year ago, at least thus far. Some of that can be traced back to the players taking on new prominence this season. Green isn't exactly known as a high-energy player. Neither is Miles Bridges, who has thus far underwhelmed following Phoenix's decision to trade an unprotected first-round pick for him over the summer.

The Suns were the feel-good story of last season. Going from that to the first team to leak displeasure to the press this season is a pretty precipitous drop. A point guard upgrade, internal or external, isn't going to address everything wrong with this team.

The Jazz are actually trying to win for the first time in the Will Hardy era... yet they're playing worse than they did when they were trying to lose. Utah's 1-5 start is the second-worst of Hardy's tenure in Utah, trailing only the six-game losing streak that kicked off their 2024-25 season. Utah's offense -- vaunted for thriving with limited resources at points during the Jazz rebuild -- is scoring fewer points per 100 possessions (105.3) than it did in any full season during the Hardy era.

The loss of the perpetually injury-prone Jaren Jackson Jr. to a torn MCL this week brought several major decisions Utah has made over the past year or so into question. The Jazz gave up three first-round picks to get Jackson on a max deal, and he's thus far given them nine games. They traded Walker Kessler and passed on Cam Boozer in the NBA Draft in part because they had Jackson. Kessler's Lakers are 5-2, and Boozer is competing with Lendeborg to become the early Rookie of the Year frontrunner. No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson has been by far the least impressive of the top four picks in June's draft thus far and was even benched down the stretch of an overtime loss to the San Antonio Spurs.

We're six games into the season. It is much too early to panic over the state of the Jazz. But after punting four full seasons to get where they are now, Utah certainly expected more than it has gotten thus far, and with Jackson injured, there's no telling when or if the Jazz will be able to turn things around.
